title: Of prayers
paragraphs: I put forward formless and unsettled fancies, as those who publish doubtful questions do to have them argued out in the schools — not to establish the truth but to seek it. And I submit them to the judgement of those whose office it is to regulate not only my writings and my actions but my very thoughts. Let what I set down here meet with correction or applause, both will be equally welcome and useful to me, since I condemn beforehand as absurd and impious anything that may be found in this rhapsody, through ignorance or oversight, contrary to the holy resolutions and prescriptions of the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church, into which I was born and in which I will die. And yet, always submitting to the authority of their censure, which has absolute power over me, I venture rashly at everything in this way, as in dealing with the present subject.

I do not know if I am wrong, but since by a particular favour of the divine bounty a certain form of prayer has been laid down and dictated to us, word by word, from the mouth of God himself, I have always thought that we ought to make more frequent use of it than we do; and if I were worth listening to, I would have Christians always use the Lord's Prayer when sitting down at table and rising from it, going to and rising from bed, and in every particular action where prayer is used — if not alone, then at least always among others. The Church may lengthen and vary prayers as the need to instruct us requires, for I know very well that in substance it is always the same and means the same thing; but this prayer ought to have such a privilege that the people should have it always on their lips. It is certain that all necessary petitions are contained in it, and that it is infinitely suitable for every occasion. It is the only prayer I use in all places and conditions, the one I keep repeating instead of changing — which is why I have no other so completely by heart.

It just came into my mind to ask where we get this habit of running to God in all our designs and undertakings, calling on him for help in every kind of business and in every place where our weakness needs support, without considering whether the occasion is just or not — invoking his name and his power whatever state we are in, whatever action we are engaged in, however vicious. He is, indeed, our sole and unique protector, and he can do anything for us; but though he is pleased to honour us with this sweet paternal alliance, he is, for all that, as just as he is good and mighty, and exercises his justice more often than his power, favouring us according to his justice and not according to our petitions.

Plato in his Laws makes three kinds of belief injurious to the gods: "that there are none; that they do not concern themselves with our affairs; that they never refuse anything to our vows, offerings, and sacrifices." The first of these errors, in his opinion, never lasted with anyone from childhood through to old age; the other two, he grants, men might dig in over.

God's justice and his power are inseparable; we call on his power in vain in an unjust cause. We are to have our souls pure and clean, at the very moment at least when we pray to him, purified from all vicious passions; otherwise we ourselves hand him the rods to chastise us with; instead of repairing the wrong we have done, we double the wickedness and the offence when we offer to the very one we are suing for pardon a heart full of disrespect and hatred. That is why I am not very ready to applaud those I see so often on their knees, when the actions nearest to the prayer do not show me some evidence of amendment and reform:
"Si, nocturnus adulter, Tempora Santonico velas adoperta cucullo."

["If, a night-time adulterer, you cover your head veiled with a Santonic cowl." — Juvenal, Sat., viii. 144. — The Santones were the people who inhabited Saintonge in France, from whom the Romans took the use of hoods or cowls covering the head and face.]

And the practice of a man who mixes devotion with a hideous life seems, in a way, more to be condemned than that of a man who is consistent with his own bent and dissolute throughout; and that is why our Church refuses entry and communion to men obstinate and incorrigible in any notorious wickedness. We pray only out of habit and for fashion's sake; or rather, we read or say our prayers out loud, which is no better than a hypocritical show of devotion. And I am scandalised to see a man cross himself three times at the Benedicite, and as often at Grace (and the more so because the sign is one I greatly revere and use continually, even when I yawn), and then dedicate every other hour of the day to acts of malice, greed, and injustice. One hour to God, the rest to the devil, as though by some arrangement and trade-off. It is a wonder to see actions so opposite to each other follow one another with such an even rhythm that they neither interfere nor disturb each other, even at the very borders and crossings from the one to the other. What a prodigious conscience that must be, that can stay quiet within itself while it harbours under the same roof, in such an agreeable and calm company, both the crime and the judge of it.

A man whose whole meditation is forever working on nothing but the very impurity he knows is so hateful to Almighty God — what is he going to say when he comes to speak to him? He draws back, but at once falls back into a relapse. If the sight of divine justice and the presence of his Maker did, as he claims, strike and chasten his soul, then however brief his repentance might be, the very fear of offending the Infinite Majesty would so often present itself to his imagination that he would soon see himself master of the vices most natural and vehement in him. But what shall we say of those who fix their whole course of life on the profit and emolument of sins they know to be mortal? How many trades and callings have we admitted and given approval to among us whose very essence is vicious? And the man who, confessing himself to me, voluntarily told me he had all his life professed and practised a religion he held to be damnable and contrary to the one he had in his heart, only to preserve his credit and the honour of his offices — how could his courage stand so disgraceful a confession? What can men say to the divine justice on such a subject?

Since their repentance would have to consist of a visible and clear restitution, they lose the option of pleading it either to God or to men. Are they so brazen as to sue for remission without satisfaction and without penitence? I see these as in the same condition as the first; but the stubbornness is not so easy to overcome here. This sudden, violent contradiction and shift of opinion they put on is a kind of miracle to me; it shows the state of an indigestible agony of mind.

It struck me as a fanciful notion in those who, in these last years, were apt to charge every man they knew to be of any extraordinary parts and who professed the Catholic religion, that his profession was only outward — maintaining further, to do him honour, of course, that whatever he might pretend to the contrary he could not, in his heart, hold anything but their reformed opinion. A nasty disorder, that a man should be so riveted to his own belief as to fancy others can believe nothing but as he does; and worse, that they should hold so vicious an opinion of such great parts as to suppose any man so qualified would prefer some present advantage of fortune to the promises of eternal life and the threats of eternal damnation. They may take my word for it: if anything could have tempted my youth, the ambition of sharing the dangers and difficulties of the late troubles would not have been the least of the motives.

It is not without very good reason, in my opinion, that the Church forbids the casual, indiscreet, and irreverent use of the holy and divine Psalms with which the Holy Ghost inspired King David. We are not to mix God into our actions except with the highest reverence and caution; that poetry is too holy to be put to no other use than exercising the lungs and pleasing the ears; it ought to come from the conscience, not from the tongue. It is not right that an apprentice in his shop, among his vain and frivolous thoughts, should be allowed to pass the time and amuse himself with such sacred things. Nor is it decent to see the Holy Book of the holy mysteries of our belief tossed about a hall or a kitchen — they used to be mysteries, but have now become sport and recreation. It is a book too serious and too venerable to be turned over carelessly or lightly; the reading of Scripture ought to be a measured and deliberate act, to which men should always add this devout preface, sursum corda, preparing even the body with so humble and composed a bearing and look as will show particular reverence and attention. Nor is it a book for everyone to handle, but for the study of select men set apart for the purpose, and whom Almighty God has been pleased to call to that office and sacred function: the wicked and the ignorant grow worse from it. It is not a tale to tell but a history to revere, fear, and adore. Are they not amusing men, then, who think they have made it fit for the people's handling by translating it into the vernacular? Does the whole understanding of what is in it hang on the words? Dare I go further and say that by drawing this near to understanding a little of it, they fall much wider of the whole scope than before? A pure and simple ignorance, wholly depending on the exposition of qualified persons, was far more learned and more salutary than this vain and verbal knowledge, which has only rashness and presumption to it.

I further believe that the liberty everyone has taken to scatter the sacred writ into so many languages carries with it far more danger than usefulness. The Jews, the Muslims, and almost all other peoples have reverentially clung to the language in which their mysteries were first conceived, and have expressly — and not without good reason — forbidden any change of them into another. Are we sure that in Biscay and in Brittany there are enough competent judges of this business to settle this translation into their own tongue? The universal Church has no harder or more solemn judgement to make. In preaching and speaking the interpretation is loose, free, mutable, and a thing in itself; so it is not the same case at all.

One of our Greek historians justly criticises the age he lived in, because the secrets of the Christian religion were scattered into the hands of every mechanic to expound and argue over as he saw fit, and says we ought to be much ashamed — we who by God's special favour enjoy the pure mysteries of piety — to let them be profaned by the ignorant rabble; considering that the pagans expressly forbade Socrates, Plato, and the other sages to inquire into or even so much as mention the things entrusted to the priests of Delphi. He says further that the factions of princes on theological subjects are armed not with zeal but with fury; that zeal springs from divine wisdom and justice and governs itself with prudence and moderation, but degenerates into hatred and envy, producing tares and nettles instead of grain and wine, when it is driven by human passions. And it was well said by another, who, advising the Emperor Theodosius, told him that disputes did not so much rock the schisms of the Church to sleep as rouse and animate heresies; that therefore all contentions and dialectical disputes were to be avoided, and men were to acquiesce wholly in the formulas of faith laid down by the ancients. And the Emperor Andronicus, having overheard some great men at high words with Lapodius in his palace about a point of ours of great importance, gave them so sharp a check as to threaten to have them thrown into the river if they did not stop. The very women and children nowadays presume to lecture the oldest and most experienced men on the ecclesiastical laws; whereas the first of those of Plato forbids them even to inquire into the civil laws, which were to stand in place of divine ordinances; and, allowing the old men to confer among themselves or with the magistrate about such things, he adds — provided it not be in the presence of the young or of profane persons.

A bishop has left it in writing that at the other end of the world there is an island, called by the ancients Dioscorides, abundantly fertile in all sorts of trees and fruits, and of an exceedingly healthful air, whose inhabitants are Christians, with churches and altars adorned only with crosses without any other images, great observers of fasts and feasts, exact payers of their tithes to the priests, and so chaste that none of them is permitted to have to do with more than one woman in his life. As for the rest, they are so content with their condition that, surrounded by the sea, they know nothing of navigation, and so simple they do not understand one syllable of the religion they profess and in which they are so devout — a thing incredible to anyone who does not know that the pagans, zealous idolaters as they are, know nothing more of their gods than their bare names and their statues. The old opening of Menalippus, a tragedy of Euripides, ran:
"O Jupiter! for that name alone Of what thou art to me is known."

I have also known, in my time, some men whose writings were faulted for being purely human and philosophical, with no admixture of theology; and yet with some show of reason the opposite case might be made — that divine doctrine, as queen and regent of the rest, better keeps her state apart; that she ought to be sovereign throughout, not subsidiary and ancillary; that perhaps grammatical, rhetorical, and logical examples may be more fittingly chosen from elsewhere, as may the material for the stage, the games, and public entertainments, than from so sacred a matter; that divine reasons are considered with greater reverence and attention by themselves and in their own proper style, than when mingled with and adapted to human discourse; that it is a fault more often noticed that the divines write too humanly than that the humanists write not theologically enough. Philosophy, says St. Chrysostom, has long been banished from the holy schools as a handmaid altogether useless and unworthy even to look in passing by the door into the sanctuary of the holy treasures of the celestial doctrine; that the human way of speaking is of a much lower form and ought not to take on for itself the dignity and majesty of divine eloquence. Let anyone who pleases talk in verbis indisciplinatis of fortune, destiny, accident, good and ill luck, and other such phrases, according to his own bent; for my part I propose fancies merely human and merely my own, and I propose them simply as human fancies, considered separately, not as settled by any decree from heaven, beyond doubt or dispute — matter of opinion, not matter of faith; things which I discuss according to my own notions, not as I believe according to God; in a lay, not a clerical fashion, and yet always in a very religious manner, as children prepare their exercises — not to instruct, but to be instructed.

And might it not be said that a decree requiring all those who are not public professors of divinity to be very reserved in writing about religion would have a strong colour of usefulness and justice — and would apply to me, among others perhaps, to hold my tongue? I have been told that even those who are not of our Church nevertheless forbid among themselves the name of God being used in common conversation, even by way of interjection, exclamation, swearing to a truth, or comparison; and I think they are right. On whatever occasion we call on God to accompany and assist us, it ought always to be done with the greatest reverence and devotion.

There is, as I remember, a passage in Xenophon where he tells us we ought to call on God so much the more seldom, the harder it is to compose our souls to the degree of calmness, patience, and devotion they ought to be in at such a time; otherwise our prayers are not only vain and fruitless but vicious. "Forgive us," we say, "our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" — what do we mean by that petition but that we are offering God a soul free of all rancour and revenge? And yet we make nothing of calling on God's assistance in our vices and inviting him into our unjust designs:
"Quae, nisi seductis, nequeas committere divis"
["Which you can only confide to the gods after you have taken them aside." — Persius, ii. 4.]

the greedy man prays for the preservation of his vain and superfluous riches; the ambitious for victory and the good running of his fortune; the thief calls on him for help in getting free of the dangers and difficulties that stand in the way of his wicked designs, or thanks him for the ease he met with in cutting a man's throat; at the door of the house men are about to storm or break into with a petard, they fall to praying for success — their hopes and intentions full of cruelty, greed, and lust.
"Hoc igitur, quo to Jovis aurem impellere tentas, Dic agedum Staio: 'proh Jupiter! O bone, clamet, Jupiter!' At sese non clamet Jupiter ipse."
["This, then, with which you try to draw the ear of Jupiter, say it to Staius. 'O Jupiter! O good Jupiter!' let him cry. Do you think Jupiter himself would not cry out upon it?" — Persius, ii. 21.]

Marguerite, Queen of Navarre, tells of a young prince — and though she does not name him, his great qualities make him easy enough to identify — who, when going on an amorous assignation to lie with the wife of a Paris lawyer, had to pass through a church on the way; he never passed that holy place going to or returning from his pious exercise without kneeling down to pray. What he could have meant to employ the divine favour for, his soul being full of such virtuous meditations, I leave to others to judge; she nevertheless cites it as evidence of singular devotion. But this is not the only proof we have that women are not very fit to handle theological matters.

A true prayer, and a genuine reconciling of ourselves to Almighty God, cannot enter an impure soul, subject at the very time of praying to the dominion of Satan. The man who calls on God for help while in a course of vice acts as a cut-purse would in calling on a magistrate to help him, or as those do who bring in the name of God to back up a lie.
"Tacito mala vota susurro Concipimus."
["We whisper our guilty prayers." — Lucan, v. 104.]
There are few men who would dare publish to the world the prayers they make to Almighty God:
"Haud cuivis promptum est, murmurque, humilesque susurros Tollere de templis, et aperto vivere voto"
["It is not easy for everyone to bring the prayers he mutters out of the temple, and to live with his wishes in the open ear of the public." — Persius, ii. 6.]
and this is why the Pythagoreans wanted prayers to be always public and heard by everyone, so people would not put forward indecent or unjust petitions, like this man:
"Clare quum dixit, Apollo! Labra movet, metuens audiri: Pulcra Laverna, Da mihi fallere, da justum sanctumque videri; Noctem peccatis, et fraudibus objice nubem."

["When he has clearly said 'Apollo!' he moves his lips, afraid to be overheard, and murmurs: O fair Laverna, give me the talent to deceive; let me appear holy and just; cover my sins with night and cast a cloud over my frauds." — Horace, Ep., i. 16, 59. — (Laverna was the goddess of thieves.)]

The gods severely punished the wicked prayers of Oedipus by granting them: he had prayed that his sons might fight out the succession to his throne between themselves, and he was wretched enough to be taken at his word. We are not to pray that everything may go as we want, but as best agrees with prudence.

It does look, in truth, as if we use our prayers as a kind of jargon, the way those do who employ holy words in sorceries and magical operations; as if we reckoned the benefit we are to draw from them as depending on the texture, sound, and jingle of the words, or on the grave composure of the face. With the soul polluted by lust, untouched by repentance, uncomforted by any recent reconciling with God, we come to present him whatever words memory hands the tongue, and from that we hope to obtain the remission of our sins. There is nothing so easy, so sweet, and so favourable as the divine law: it calls us and invites us to her, guilty and abominable as we are; she stretches out her arms and takes us into her bosom, foul and polluted as we are now and as we are for the future to be. But in return we are to look on her with a reverent eye; we are to receive this pardon with all gratitude and submission, and at that instant, at least, when we address ourselves to her, to have a soul sensitive to the wrongs we have done and at enmity with the passions that drew us to offend her. Neither the gods, says Plato, nor good men will accept the gift of a wicked man:
"Immunis aram si terigit manus, Non sumptuosa blandior hostia Mollivit aversos Penates Farre pio et saliente mica."

["If a pure hand has touched the altar, the modest offering of a small cake and a few grains of salt will appease the offended household gods more effectually than the most costly sacrifices." — Horace, Od., iii. 23, 17.]

title: Of age
paragraphs: I cannot accept the way we set down the length of our life for ourselves. I notice that the sages cut it back considerably from the common opinion. "What," said the younger Cato to those who would have stopped his hand from killing himself, "am I now of an age to be reproached that I am leaving the world too soon?" And yet he was only forty-eight. He thought that a ripe and advanced age, considering how few reach it. And those who, soothing themselves with I don't know what course of nature, promise themselves some years beyond that, might have some reason for it if they could be exempted from the endless number of accidents to which we are naturally exposed. What an idle notion it is to expect to die of a decay of strength — which is the effect of extreme old age — and to set ourselves no shorter span of life than that, when it is a kind of death rarer than any other and very seldom seen. We call only that a natural death — as if it were contrary to nature to see a man break his neck in a fall, drown in a shipwreck, be carried off by a pleurisy or a plague, and as if our ordinary condition did not expose us to these mishaps. Let us not flatter ourselves any longer with these fine words; we ought, perhaps, rather to call that natural which is general, common, and universal.

To die of old age is a death rare, extraordinary, and singular, and so much less natural than the others; it is the last and outermost sort of dying, and the more remote, the less to be hoped for. It is indeed the bourn beyond which we are not to pass, and which the law of nature has set as a limit not to be exceeded; but it is, also, a privilege she is rarely seen to grant us, that of lasting that long. It is a lease she signs only as a particular favour, and perhaps to only one man in the space of two or three generations, and even then with a pass to boot, to carry him through all the obstacles and difficulties she has strewn in the way of so long a course. And so my opinion is that once we have reached forty we should think of it as an age very few arrive at. Since men do not normally get that far, it is a sign we are already well advanced; and since we have gone past the usual bounds, which are the proper measure of life, we ought not to count on going much further. Having escaped so many precipices of death, into which we have seen so many other men fall, we should acknowledge that an extraordinary fortune like the one that has so far carried us through those high perils and kept us alive beyond the ordinary span of living is not likely to last long.

There is a fault in our very laws for upholding this error: they say a man is not capable of managing his own estate until he is twenty-five years old, when he will be hard pressed to manage his life that long. Augustus cut five years off the old Roman standard and declared that thirty was enough for a judge. Servius Tullius released the knights over forty-seven from the fatigues of war; Augustus released them at forty-five — though it seems a little unreasonable to me that men should be sent to the fireside until fifty-five or sixty. I would have our calling and employment extended as far as possible for the public good; and the fault, I think, is on the other side — they do not employ us early enough. This emperor was arbiter of the whole world at nineteen, and yet would have a man be thirty before he could be fit to settle a dispute about a gutter.

For my part I believe our souls are as adult at twenty as they are ever likely to be, and as capable then as ever. A soul that has not by then given clear evidence of its force and virtue will never come to proof afterwards. The natural qualities and virtues bring forth what they have of vigour and finesse within that span or never,
"Si l'espine rion picque quand nai, A pene que picque jamai,"
If the thorn does not prick at birth, it will hardly ever prick at all.
as they say in the Dauphiné.

Of all the great human actions I have ever heard or read of, of whatever kind, I have noticed, both in former ages and in our own, that more were performed before the age of thirty than after — and often within the very lives of the same men. May I not confidently point to those of Hannibal and his great rival Scipio? The better half of their lives they lived off the glory they had won in their youth: great men afterwards, true — in comparison with others; but by no means in comparison with themselves. As for my own case, I do certainly believe that since that age both my understanding and my constitution have rather decayed than improved, and gone back rather than forward. It is possible, with those who make the best use of their time, that knowledge and experience grow with their years; but vivacity, quickness, steadiness, and other pieces of us of much greater importance, and much more essentially our own, languish and decay:
"Ubi jam validis quassatum est viribus aevi Corpus, et obtusis ceciderunt viribus artus, Claudicat ingenium, delirat linguaque, mensque."
["Once the body is shaken by the violence of time, with blood and vigour ebbing away, the judgement halts, and tongue and mind dote." — Lucretius, iii. 452.]

Sometimes the body gives way to age first, sometimes the mind; and I have seen plenty whose brains weakened before either their legs or their stomach. And since it is a disease of no great pain to the sufferer, and of obscure symptoms, the danger is so much the greater. For this reason I complain of our laws — not that they keep us at our work too long, but that they put us to work too late. Considering the frailty of life and how many ordinary and natural rocks it is exposed to, we should not surrender so large a share of it to childhood, idleness, and apprenticeship.

[Which Cotton renders thus: "Birth, though noble, ought not to take up so large a vacancy, and so tedious a course of education." Florio (1613) makes the passage read as follows: "Methinks that, considering the weakness of our life, and seeing the infinite number of ordinary rocks and natural dangers it is subject to, we should not, as soon as we come into the world, allot so large a share of it to unprofitable wantonness in youth, ill-bred idleness, and slow-learning apprenticeship."]

title: Of the inconstancy of our actions
paragraphs: Those who make it their business to scrutinise human actions find nothing so confounding as the effort to reconcile them and present them to the world with one consistent lustre and reputation; for they commonly contradict one another so strangely that it seems impossible they could proceed from one and the same person. We find the younger Marius one moment a son of Mars, the next a son of Venus. Pope Boniface VIII, it is said, entered his papacy like a fox, conducted himself in it like a lion, and died like a dog. And who could believe it was the same Nero, the very image of cruelty, who, having the sentence of a condemned man brought to him to sign, as was the custom, cried out, "Oh that I had never been taught to write!" — so much did it grieve him to condemn a man to death? History is full of such examples, and every man can produce so many from his own practice or observation that I sometimes wonder to see thoughtful men go to the trouble of sorting these pieces, when irresolution appears to me the most common and obvious vice of our nature — witness the famous line of the playwright Publius:
"Malum consilium est, quod mutari non potest."
["It is bad counsel that admits of no change." — Publius Mimus, in Aulus Gellius, xvii. 14.]

There seems some reason in forming a judgment of a man from the most usual habits of his life; but, given the natural instability of our manners and opinions, I have often thought even the best authors a little off in trying so stubbornly to make us out as a constant and solid weave. They settle on a general character and interpret all his actions accordingly, and any that cannot be bent into uniformity with the rest are at once put down to dissimulation. Augustus has escaped them, for there was in him so plain, so sudden, so continual a variety throughout his whole life that he has slipped past the most daring critics undecided. I find it harder to believe in a man's constancy than in any other virtue, and easier to believe in its opposite. He who would judge a man in detail and bit by bit would more often be able to speak the truth. It is hard, in all of antiquity, to pick out a dozen men who have shaped their lives to one fixed and constant course — which is the chief design of wisdom. As one of the ancients says, summing the whole business in a word, all the rules of human life come down to this: "to will, and not to will, always one and the same thing. I will not add," he says, "'provided the will be just,' for if it is not just, it cannot possibly be always one." I learned long ago that vice is nothing but irregularity and want of measure, and so it is impossible to attach constancy to it. As Demosthenes says, "the beginning of all virtue is consultation and deliberation; the end and perfection of it is constancy." If we wished to settle on any fixed course by reason, we would pitch on the best — but no one has thought of it:
"Quod petit, spernit; repetit, quod nuper omisit; AEstuat, et vitae disconvenit ordine toto."
["What he sought he despises; what he lately gave up he seeks again. He is in a ferment, and inconsistent in the whole order of his life." — Horace, Ep., i. 1, 98.]

Our ordinary practice is to follow the leanings of our appetite, left or right, up or down, as we are carried by the breath of occasion. We never think what we want until the moment we want it, and we change like that little creature that takes its colour from whatever it is set on. What we proposed to ourselves just now we change at once, and then go straight back to it; it is nothing but shifting and inconsistency:
"Ducimur, ut nervis alienis mobile lignum."
["We are pulled about like the puppet by another's strings." — Horace, Sat., ii. 7, 82.]
We do not go, we are driven; like things that float, sometimes leisurely, sometimes violently, according to the calm or rush of the current:
"Nonne videmus, Quid sibi quisque velit, nescire, et quaerere semper Commutare locum, quasi onus deponere possit?"
["Do we not see them, unsure what they want, always trying to change their place, as if they could lay down the burden?" — Lucretius, iii. 1070.]
Every day a new fancy, and our moods march in time with the weather.
"Tales sunt hominum mentes, quali pater ipse Juppiter auctificas lustravit lumine terras."
["The minds of men are such that they change with the light by which father Jupiter himself has lit up the teeming earth." — Cicero, Frag. Poet., lib. x.]

We fluctuate between various inclinations; we will nothing freely, nothing absolutely, nothing constantly. In any man who had set down clear laws and rules in his head for his own conduct, we would notice a steadiness of manner, an order, a sure relation of one thing and action to another, shining through his whole life. Empedocles observed this very disparity in the people of Agrigentum: they gave themselves up to pleasure as if every day were their last and built as if they were going to live forever. The judgment is not hard to make, as is very evident in the younger Cato; whoever has found one step in him will be led to all the rest — it is a harmony of perfectly tuned notes that cannot jar. With us it is quite the opposite: every particular action requires a particular judgment. The surest course to steer by, in my opinion, would be to take our measure from the nearest related circumstances, without engaging in a longer inquiry or drawing any larger conclusion. I was told, during the civil disorders of our poor kingdom, that a girl, near where I was then staying, had thrown herself out of a window to avoid being forced by a common soldier billeted in the house. She was not killed by the fall, and so, repeating her attempt, she would have cut her own throat had she not been stopped. Still, having wounded herself enough to look in real danger, she freely confessed that the soldier had so far only pestered her with courtship, urgent solicitation, and gifts, but that she was afraid he would in the end resort to violence — all of which she delivered with such a look and accent, soaked moreover in her own blood (the highest testimony of her virtue), that she seemed another Lucretia. Yet I have since been well assured that, both before and after, she was not such a difficult piece. And, as the innkeeper says in Ariosto, however handsome a man and worthy a gentleman you may be, do not conclude too much about your mistress's inviolable chastity just because you were turned away — for all you know, she may have a better stomach for your muleteer.

Antigonus, having taken one of his soldiers into great favour and esteem for his courage, gave his physicians strict orders to cure him of a long inward illness he had languished under. Noticing afterwards that the cured man went about his work much more coldly than before, he asked him what had so altered and cowed him. "You yourself, sir," he replied, "by relieving me of the pains that made me weary of life." Likewise, one of Lucullus's soldiers, having been robbed by the enemy, performed a brave exploit on them in revenge by which he came out the gainer. Lucullus, having taken a good opinion of him from that action, tried to engage him in an enterprise of very great danger, with all the persuasions and promises he could think of —
"Verbis, quae timido quoque possent addere mentem,"
["Words that might add courage even to a timid man." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2, 1, 2.]
"Get some poor plundered soldier," he answered, "to do that job":
"Quantumvis rusticus, ibit, Ibit eo, quo vis, qui zonam perdidit, inquit;"
["Some poor wretch who has lost his purse, he said, will go wherever you want him to." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2, 39.]

— and flatly refused to go. When we read that Mahomet furiously berated Chasan, commander of the Janissaries, because he had seen the Hungarians break into his squadrons and Chasan had behaved badly in the business, and that Chasan, instead of any other answer, rushed alone, scimitar in hand, into the first body of the enemy, where he was promptly cut to pieces — we should perhaps look on that act not so much as vindication as a sudden turn of mind, not so much natural valour as sudden spite. The man you saw yesterday so daring and brave, do not be surprised to see as great a coward the next day: anger, necessity, company, wine, or the sound of the trumpet had roused his spirits. This is no valour formed and settled by reason, but accidentally produced by circumstances, and so it is no wonder if, under contrary circumstances, it shows up as quite another thing.

These pliant variations and contradictions, so obvious in us, have led some to believe man has two souls — others, two distinct powers that always accompany us and lean us one way or the other, the one toward good, the other toward evil, by their own nature and bent; so abrupt a variety not being thinkable as flowing from one and the same source.

For my part, the gust of every accident not only carries me along with it according to its own slope, but I also disturb and trouble myself by the instability of my own posture; and whoever looks closely into his own breast will hardly find himself twice in the same condition. I give my soul sometimes one face and sometimes another, depending on which side I turn her to. If I speak variously of myself, it is because I see myself variously; all the contraries are to be found there in one corner or another, in one fashion or another: bashful, brazen; chaste, lustful; chattering, silent; hardworking, fastidious; clever, dull; melancholy, cheerful; lying, truthful; learned, ignorant; generous, miserly, and prodigal. I find all this in myself, more or less, as I turn myself around; and whoever sifts himself thoroughly will find in himself, even in his own judgment, this volatility and discord. I have nothing to say of myself entirely, simply, and solidly, without mixture and confusion. "Distinguo" is the most universal limb of my logic. Though I always intend to speak well of good things, and rather to interpret what happens in the best light than otherwise, yet such is the strangeness of our condition that we are often pushed to do well even by vice itself, if doing well were not measured by intention alone. One gallant action, therefore, ought not to prove a man brave; if a man were really brave, he would be so always, and on all occasions. If it were a habit of valour and not a sudden burst, it would make a man equally resolute in every kind of trouble — the same alone as in company, the same in the duelling field as in battle. For say what they will, there is not one valour for the pavement and another for the field; he would bear sickness in his bed as bravely as a wound in the field, and fear death no more in his own house than at an assault. We would not then see the same man charge a breach with brave confidence and afterwards torment himself like a woman over the loss of a lawsuit or the death of a child. When a man is an infamous coward yet firm in the necessities of poverty, when he shrinks from a barber's razor and rushes fearlessly on the swords of the enemy, the action is to be praised, not the man.
Many of the Greeks, says Cicero, cannot bear the sight of an enemy yet are brave in sickness; the Cimbrians and Celtiberians quite the opposite:
"Nihil enim potest esse aequabile, quod non a certa ratione proficiscatur."
["Nothing can be uniform that does not proceed from a fixed ground of reason." — Cicero, ibid., c. 26.]

No valour can be more extreme of its kind than Alexander's; but it is of just one kind, not full enough throughout, not universal. Incomparable as it is, it has its blemishes. His being so often at his wits' end on the slightest suspicion of his captains plotting against his life, and conducting that inquiry with so much vehemence and rash injustice, with a fear that wrecked his natural reason — that is one telling instance. And the superstition with which he was so tainted carries with it a certain image of cowardice; the excess of his remorse over the killing of Clytus is another testimony to the unevenness of his courage. All we perform is no more than a patchwork, so to speak, of various pieces, and we would acquire honour under a false title. Virtue cannot be followed except for itself; if it sometimes borrows her mask for some other purpose, she promptly tears it off again. It is a vivid and powerful tint that, once the soul has truly absorbed it, will not come out except with the cloth. And so, to judge a man rightly, we must follow his trace long and with close observation. If constancy does not stand firm there on her own proper base —
"Cui vivendi via considerata atque provisa est,"
["For whom the path of life has been carefully considered and laid out." — Cicero, Paradox, v. 1.]

— if the variety of events makes him alter his pace (his path, I mean, for the pace may be faster or slower), let him go: such a man runs before the wind, "Avau le dent," as the motto of our Talebot has it.

It is no wonder, says one of the ancients, that chance has such a dominion over us, since it is by chance that we live. It is not possible for anyone who has not designed his life for some certain end — it is impossible for anyone to arrange the pieces — who has not the whole form already worked out in his imagination. What use are colours to a man who does not know what he is to paint? No one sets down a clear design for his life; we only deliberate over it in pieces. The archer must first know what he is to aim at, and then fit his arm, bow, string, shaft, and motion to it; our intentions stray and wander because they are not aimed at any settled end. No wind serves the man who sets sail for no particular harbour. I cannot accept the judgment given by someone on Sophocles' behalf, who concluded that he was capable of managing his domestic affairs, against the charge brought by his son, simply from reading one of his tragedies.

Nor do I accept the inference of the Parians sent to settle the affairs of the Milesians as sufficient for the conclusion they drew from it: coming to inspect the island, they noted the fields that were best tended and the country-houses best run; and, having taken the names of the owners, when they had assembled the citizens, they appointed those farmers as new governors and magistrates — concluding that men who had been so careful in their own private affairs would be so in the public ones too. We are all lumps, of so varied and shapeless a weave that every piece plays its own game every moment, and there is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others:
"Magnam rem puta, unum hominem agere."
["Reckon it a great thing to act always as one and the same man." — Seneca, Ep., 150.]

Since ambition can teach a man valour, temperance, and generosity, and even justice too; since avarice can inspire in a shop-boy, bred and nursed in obscurity and ease, the courage to expose himself so far from the fireside to the mercy of the waves and angry Neptune in a frail boat; since it can further teach him discretion and prudence; and since even Venus can inflate boys still under the discipline of the rod with boldness and resolve, and pour masculine courage into the heart of tender virgins in their mothers' arms —
"Hac duce, custodes furtim transgressa jacentes, Ad juvenem tenebris sola puella venit:"
["With her as guide, the maiden, slipping furtively past the lounging guards, goes alone in the darkness to the young man." — Tibullus, ii. 2, 75.]

— it is no business simply for the understanding to judge us by our outward actions; it must penetrate the very soul, and there discover by what springs the motion is steered. But because that is a high and risky undertaking, I could wish that fewer would attempt it.

title: Of drunkenness
paragraphs: The world is nothing but variety and dissimilarity. Vices are all alike in that they are vices, and perhaps the Stoics understand them that way; but, even though they are equally vices, they are not all equal vices. The man who has gone a hundred paces beyond the ordinary bounds —
"Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum,"
["Beyond or short of which the right cannot exist." — Horace, Sat., i. 1, 107.]
— should not be in a worse condition than the man who has gone only ten beyond; and the idea that sacrilege is no worse than stealing a cabbage is not to be believed:
"Nec vincet ratio hoc, tantumdem ut peccet, idemque, Qui teneros caules alieni fregerit horti, Et qui nocturnus divum sacra legerit."

There is as much diversity in this as in anything whatever. To confound the order and measure of sins is dangerous: murderers, traitors, and tyrants gain too much by it, and it is not reasonable that they should soothe their consciences just because another man is idle, lecherous, or lax in his devotions. Each man rates the offences of his neighbours high while making excuses for his own. Our very teachers sometimes rank them, in my opinion, very badly. As Socrates said that the chief office of wisdom is to distinguish good from evil, so we — whose very best are vicious — ought to say the same of the science of distinguishing between one vice and another; without which, and that very exactly performed, the virtuous and the wicked will remain mixed up and unrecognisable.

Now, among the rest, drunkenness seems to me a gross and brutish vice. The soul has a greater share in the others, and there are some vices that have something — if one may say so — of the generous in them; vices in which there is a mixture of knowledge, diligence, valour, prudence, dexterity, and address. This one is wholly bodily and earthly. And the rudest nation in Europe today is the only one where it is in fashion. Other vices unsettle the understanding; this one totally overthrows it and stupefies the body:
"Cum vini vis penetravit . . . Consequitur gravitas membrorum, praepediuntur Crura vacillanti, tardescit lingua, madet mens, Nant oculi; clamor, singultus, jurgia, gliscunt."

["When the force of wine has penetrated us, a heaviness of the limbs follows; the legs of the staggering man fail him; the tongue grows sluggish, the mind is clouded, the eyes swim; noise, hiccups, and quarrels arise." — Lucretius, i. 3, 475.]

The worst state of man is the one in which he loses the knowledge and the government of himself. It is said, among other things on this subject, that just as the must fermenting in a vessel works up to the top whatever it has at the bottom, so wine, in those who have drunk beyond measure, vents the most inward secrets:
"Tu sapientum Curas et arcanum jocoso Consilium retegis Lyaeo."
["You unveil to merry Lyaeus the cares and secret counsels of the wise." — Horace, Od., iii. 21, 14.]
[Lyaeus, a name given to Bacchus.]

Josephus tells us that by giving an ambassador the enemy had sent him a full dose of liquor, he wormed his secrets out of him. And yet, Augustus, entrusting his most inward state affairs to Lucius Piso (who conquered Thrace), never found him at fault in the slightest — any more than Tiberius did with Cossus, to whom he confided all his counsels — though we know both of them were so given to drink that they often had to be carried out of the Senate dead drunk:
"Hesterno inflatum venas ut semper, Lyaeo."
["Their veins still swollen, as usual, with yesterday's wine." — Virgil, Ecl., vi. 15.]
And the plot to kill Caesar was as safely entrusted to Cimber, though he was often drunk, as to Cassius, who drank nothing but water.
[On which Cassius pleasantly remarked: "What, am I to put up with a tyrant — I who can't put up with wine?"]
We see our Germans, drunk as devils, still know their post, remember the password, and keep to their ranks:
"Nec facilis victoria de madidis, et Blaesis, atque mero titubantibus."
["Nor is victory easily had over men so drunk they can scarcely speak or stand." — Juvenal, Sat., xv. 47.]

I would not have believed there could be so deep, senseless, and dead a degree of drunkenness if I had not read in history that Attalus, in order to put a notable insult upon him, invited to supper the same Pausanias who afterwards killed Philip of Macedon — a king whose excellent qualities testified well enough to his education in the household and company of Epaminondas — and made him drink to such a pitch that he could afterwards hand over his beauty, as if he were a roadside whore, to the muleteers and the basest servants of the house. And I have been further told, by a lady whom I highly honour and esteem, that near Bordeaux and around Castres, where she lives, a countrywoman, a widow of chaste reputation, finding in herself the first signs of pregnancy, told her neighbours innocently that if she had a husband she would think herself with child. But as the grounds for suspicion grew daily, until at last it became plain fact, the poor woman was driven to have it proclaimed in her parish church that whoever had done the deed and would freely confess could not only be forgiven but, if he liked, married. Whereupon a young fellow who served her as a labourer, encouraged by the proclamation, declared that one holiday he had found her — having taken too much of the bottle — so fast asleep by the fireplace and in so indecent a posture that he could conveniently do his business without waking her. And they live to this day as man and wife.

It is true that antiquity has not much condemned this vice; the writings even of several philosophers speak very softly about it, and even among the Stoics there are some who advise people to allow themselves now and then the freedom to drink, even to drunkenness, in order to refresh the soul:
"Hoc quoque virtutum quondam certamine, magnum Socratem palmam promeruisse ferunt."
["In this contest of virtues too, they say, the great Socrates once earned the palm." — Cornelius Gallus, Ep., i. 47.]
That censor and reprover of others, Cato, was reproached for being a hard drinker:
"Narratur et prisci Catonis Saepe mero caluisse virtus."
["And of old Cato it is said that his courage was often warmed with wine." — Horace, Od., iii. 21, 11. — Cato the Elder.]

Cyrus, that famous king, urged this excellence among the qualities by which he claimed precedence over his brother Artaxerxes — that he could drink a great deal more than he. And in the best-governed nations this contest of skill in drinking is much in use. I have heard Silvius, an excellent physician of Paris, say that the digestive faculties of the stomach, lest they grow idle, are not amiss to rouse once a month by this excess, and to spur them lest they become dull and rusty. And one author tells us that the Persians used to deliberate on their most important affairs after being well warmed with wine.

My taste and constitution are greater enemies to this vice than my reasoning is; for besides that I easily submit my belief to the authority of ancient opinions, I do view it as an unmanly and stupid vice, but less malicious and harmful than the others, which almost all jostle public society more directly. And if we cannot please ourselves without some cost, as they hold, I find this vice costs a man's conscience less than the others, and besides it is no trouble to prepare and not hard to come by — a consideration not altogether to be despised. A man well advanced in both rank and age, listing for me the three main pleasures still left to him in life, counted this as one; and where would a man more justly find it than among the natural comforts? But he did not quite take it the right way, for delicacy and the curious choice of wines are to be avoided here. If you base your pleasure on drinking the best, you condemn yourself to the penance of drinking the worst. Your taste must be more indifferent and free; so refined a palate is not required to make a good drinker. The Germans drink almost indifferently of all wines with delight; their business is to pour down, not to taste — and it is so much the better for them: their pleasure is so much the more plentiful and nearer at hand.

Secondly, to drink in the French manner — only at the two meals, and then moderately — is to be too sparing of the god's favours. More time and constancy are required than that. The ancients spent whole nights at this exercise, often adding the next day to eke it out; and so we ought to take greater liberty and stick closer to our work. I have seen a great lord of my time — a man of high enterprise and famous success — who, without setting himself to it, and going at his usual rate of drinking at meals, drank not much less than five quarts of wine, and at his going away appeared only too wise and shrewd, to the harm of our business. The pleasure we count on for the course of our lives ought to have a greater share of our time dedicated to it; like shop-boys and labourers we should refuse no occasion or omit any chance of drinking, and always have it in mind. It seems to me that every day we shorten and curtail the use of wine, and that the morning drams, mid-meal pulls, and snacks I used to see in my father's house when I was a boy were more usual and frequent then than they are now.

Is it that we pretend to a reformation? Truly, no. But perhaps we are more devoted to Venus than our fathers were. These are two exercises that hinder each other in their vigour. Lechery weakens our stomach on one side, and on the other sobriety renders us smarter and more amorous for love's exercise.

It is wonderful what strange stories I have heard my father tell of the chastity of the age in which he lived. It was for him to say it, being by art and nature cut out and finished for the service of ladies. He spoke well and little, ever mixing his language with some illustration out of the authors then in fashion, especially Spanish, and among the Spanish the man they called Marcus Aurelius was usually in his mouth. His bearing was gently grave, humble, and very modest; he was very particular about neatness and propriety in his person and clothes, whether on horseback or on foot; he was extraordinarily exact in keeping his word; and his conscience and religion tended rather toward superstition than otherwise. For a man of small stature, he was very strong, well-proportioned and well-knit, with a pleasing complexion inclining to brown, and very skilled in all noble exercises. I have still in the house canes weighted with lead, with which they say he exercised his arms for throwing the bar or stone, or in fencing, and shoes with leaden soles to make him lighter for running or leaping. Of his vaulting he has left little marvels behind: I have seen him, when past sixty, laugh at our exercises, throw himself in his furred gown into the saddle, walk the table on his thumbs, and hardly ever climb the stairs to his chamber without taking three or four steps at a time. As for what I was saying before, he said there was scarcely one woman of quality of bad repute in the whole province. He told strange confidences — some of them his own — of virtuous women, free from any suspicion of ill; and for his own part, he solemnly swore he was a virgin at his marriage, and that after a long stretch of soldiering beyond the mountains, of which wars he left us a journal in his own hand, where he gave a precise point-by-point account of everything that happened, both public and personal. And he was moreover married at a very ripe maturity, in the year 1528, the thirty-third year of his age, on his way home from Italy. But let us get back to our bottles.

The discomforts of old age, which need some refreshment and support, might reasonably breed in me a desire for this faculty, since it is, as it were, the last pleasure the course of years deprives us of. Natural heat, say the good fellows, first lodges in the feet — that concerns infancy; from there it climbs into the middle region, where it stays a long time and produces, in my opinion, the only true pleasures of human life (all other pleasures by comparison are asleep); toward the end, like a vapour rising upward, it arrives at the throat, where it takes its final lodging and ends the journey. I do not, however, understand how a man can stretch the pleasure of drinking beyond his thirst and forge in his imagination an appetite artificial and against nature. My stomach would not go that far: it has enough to do dealing with what it takes in for its own necessity. My constitution is not to bother with drink except as it follows eating, and to wash down my meat; for which reason my last draught is always the largest. And since in old age our palate is furred with phlegm or distorted by some other ill, wine tastes better to us the cleaner-washed and more open the pores are. At least, I seldom taste the first glass well. Anacharsis wondered that the Greeks drank from larger glasses toward the end of a meal than at the beginning — which was, I suppose, for the same reason the Germans do the same, since they only then begin their drinking battle in earnest.

Plato forbids wine to children before eighteen, and getting drunk before forty; but after forty, he lets them please themselves and mix into their feasts a generous touch of Dionysus, that good deity who restores to younger men their gaiety and to old men their youth; who softens the passions of the soul, as iron is softened by fire; and in his Laws he allows such merry gatherings as good and very useful, provided they have a sober chairman to govern them and keep order — drunkenness being, he says, a true and certain test of every man's nature, and besides fit to inspire old men with the spirit to enjoy themselves in dancing and music, things of great use that they will not dare attempt when sober. He further says that wine can supply the soul with temperance and the body with health. Nevertheless, these restrictions, partly borrowed from the Carthaginians, please him: that men hold back from excess in military campaigns; that every judge and magistrate abstain from it when about his official duties or the consideration of public affairs; that the day is not to be spent on it, that being a time owed to other occupations; nor the night on which a man intends to beget children.

It is said that the philosopher Stilpo, weighed down by old age, deliberately hastened his end by drinking pure wine. The same thing — though not by his own design — dispatched the philosopher Arcesilaus too.
But it is an old and pleasant question whether the soul of a wise man can be overcome by the strength of wine?
"Si munitae adhibet vim sapientiae."

To what vanity does the good opinion we have of ourselves drive us? The most disciplined and most perfect soul in the world has more than enough to do to keep itself upright and not be overthrown by its own weakness. There is not one in a thousand that is right and settled even one minute in a whole lifetime, and one might well doubt whether, according to her natural condition, she ever can be; but to add constancy to that is her utmost perfection — by which I mean when nothing comes along to jolt and unsettle her, which a thousand accidents may do. It is to little purpose that the great poet Lucretius makes such a clatter with his philosophy, when — behold! — he goes mad with a love potion. Is it to be imagined that a stroke will not stun Socrates as well as a porter? Some men have forgotten their own names through the violence of a disease; and a slight wound has turned the judgment of others upside down. Let him be as wise as he will, after all he is still a man — and than that what is there more frail, more wretched, or more nothing? Wisdom does not override our natural dispositions:
"Sudores itaque, et pallorem exsistere toto Corpore, et infringi linguam, vocemque aboriri, Caligare oculos, sonere aures, succidere artus, Demque concidere, ex animi terrore, videmus."

["Sweat and pallor come over the whole body, the tongue is rendered powerless, the voice dies away, the eyes are darkened, the ears ring, the limbs sink under us from the influence of fear." — Lucretius, iii. 155.]

He must shut his eyes against the blow that threatens him; he must tremble on the edge of a precipice, like a child — nature having kept back these light marks of her authority, not to be overridden by our reason and Stoic virtue, to teach man his mortality and our weakness. He turns pale with fear, red with shame, and groans with colic, if not in a desperate cry, at least in a hoarse and broken voice:
"Humani a se nihil alienum putet."
["Let him not think himself exempt from anything that befalls men in general." — Terence, Heauton, i. 1, 25.]
The poets, who feign all things at pleasure, dare not absolve their greatest heroes of tears:
"Sic fatur lacrymans, classique immittit habenas."
["Thus he speaks, weeping, and then sets sail with his fleet." — Aeneid, vi. 1.]

It is enough for a man to curb and moderate his inclinations; to suppress them entirely is not in him. Even our great Plutarch, that excellent and perfect judge of human actions, when he sees Brutus and Torquatus kill their children, begins to wonder whether virtue could go so far, and to question whether these men were not rather driven by some other passion. All actions that go beyond the ordinary bounds are open to sinister interpretation, since our liking holds no better with what is above than with what is below it.
Let us leave aside that other sect that openly professes a scornful superiority; but when, even in the sect reputed the most quiet and gentle, we hear these boasts of Metrodorus —
"Occupavi te, Fortuna, atque cepi: omnesque aditus tuos interclusi ut ad me aspirare non posses;"
["Fortune, I have got the better of you, and have so blocked all your approaches that you cannot reach me." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 9.]

— when Anaxarchus, on the order of Nicocreon, tyrant of Cyprus, was placed in a stone mortar and pounded with iron mauls, never stopped saying, "Strike, batter, break — it is not Anaxarchus, it is only his sheath you pound and crush"; when we hear our martyrs cry out to the tyrant from the middle of the flame, "This side is roasted enough — fall to and eat, it is well done; now set to work on the other"; when we hear the child in Josephus, torn piecemeal with pincers, defy Antiochus and cry out in a steady, assured voice, "Tyrant, you waste your effort — I am still at ease. Where is the pain? Where are the torments with which you so threatened me? Is this all you can do? My constancy torments you more than your cruelty does me. Pitiful coward, you weaken and I grow stronger; make me complain, make me bend, make me yield if you can; encourage your guards, cheer up your executioners — see, see, they faint and can do no more; arm them, goad them, spur them on" — one must confess that there is some frenzy, some fury, however holy, possessing those souls at such a moment. When we come to these Stoical sallies — "I had rather be mad than voluptuous," says Antisthenes; when Sextius tells us he had rather be fettered by affliction than by pleasure; when Epicurus presumes to play with his gout, and, refusing health and ease, defies all torments, despising the lesser pains as beneath his contest, hungering and calling out for others sharper, more violent, and more worthy of him —
"Spumantemque dari, pecora inter inertia, votis Optat aprum, aut fulvum descendere monte leonem:"
["And instead of timid beasts, he wishes the foaming boar or the tawny lion would come down from the mountain." — Aeneid, iv. 158.]

— who but must conclude that these are wild sallies driven by a courage that has broken loose from its place? Our soul cannot reach so high from her own seat; she must leave it, raise herself up, and, taking the bridle in her teeth, carry her man so far that he is afterwards astonished himself at what he has done — just as, in war, the heat of battle drives generous soldiers to perform things of such infinite danger that, recollecting them afterwards, they are themselves the first to wonder; as it is also with the poets, who are often seized with admiration of their own writings and do not know where to find again the track by which they ran so fine a course — which in them is also called fury and rapture. As Plato says, it is no use for a sober-minded man to knock at the door of poetry; so Aristotle says no excellent soul is exempt from a mixture of madness; and he has reason to call all transports, however commendable, that surpass our own judgment and understanding, madness, since wisdom is a regular government of the soul, conducted with measure and proportion, and for which she is answerable to herself. Plato argues thus, that the faculty of prophesying is so far above us that we must be out of ourselves when we meddle with it, and our prudence must either be obstructed by sleep or sickness, or lifted from its place by some celestial rapture.

title: A custom of the isle of Cea
paragraphs: [Cos. Cea is the form of the name given by Pliny.]

If to philosophise is, as it is defined, to doubt, then much more should writing at random and playing the fool, as I do, be reckoned doubting; for it is for novices and freshmen to inquire and dispute, and for the chairman to moderate and decide.
My moderator is the authority of the divine will, which governs us without contradiction, and is seated above these human and vain disputations.

When Philip had forcibly entered the Peloponnese and someone said to Damidas that the Lacedaemonians stood likely to suffer greatly if they did not in time reconcile themselves to his favour, "Why, you wretched fellow," he replied, "what can they suffer who do not fear to die?" Agis, too, was asked how a man might live free. "Why," he said, "by despising death." These, and a thousand other sayings to the same effect, plainly mean more than patiently awaiting the stroke of death when it comes — for there are several accidents of life worse to suffer than death itself. Witness the Lacedaemonian boy captured by Antigonus and sold as a slave who, when his master ordered him to some base task, said, "You shall see whom you have bought — it would be a shame for me to serve, when liberty is within my reach," and so saying, threw himself from the top of the house. When Antipater severely threatened the Lacedaemonians, the better to bring them to grant a demand of his, they replied, "If you threaten us with worse than death, we shall die more willingly"; and to Philip, who had written that he would frustrate all their undertakings, "What, will you also stop us from dying?" This is the meaning of the saying that the wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can; and that the most obliging present nature has given us, and which removes all colour for complaining of our condition, is that she has placed the keys of life in our own keeping. She has provided only one door into life, but a hundred thousand ways out. We may be cramped for earth to live on, but earth enough to die on can never be wanting, as Boiocalus answered the Romans. Why complain of this world? It does not detain you; your own cowardice is the cause if you live in pain. There needs no more to die than to will to die:
"Ubique mors est; optime hoc cavit deus. Eripere vitam nemo non homini potest; At nemo mortem; mille ad hanc aditus patent."
["Death is everywhere: heaven has well provided for that. Anyone can deprive us of life; no one can deprive us of death. To death there are a thousand approaches." — Seneca, Thebais, i. 151.]

Nor is it a remedy for one disease only; death is the sure cure of all. It is a most assured harbour that is never to be feared and very often to be sought. It is all one whether a man gives himself his end or waits to receive it by some other means — whether he pays before his day or stays till his day of payment comes; from wherever it comes, it is still his. In whatever part the thread breaks, that is the end of the skein. The most voluntary death is the finest. Life depends on the pleasure of others; death on our own. We should suit ourselves in nothing so much as in this. Reputation is not concerned in such an undertaking; it is folly to be troubled by any such worry. Living is slavery if the freedom to die is lacking. The ordinary cure is carried on at the expense of life: they torment us with cauteries, incisions, and amputations; they cut off our food and drain our blood; one step further and we are cured indeed and effectively. Why is not the jugular vein as much at our disposal as the median? For a desperate disease, a desperate cure. Servius the grammarian, tormented with gout, could think of no better remedy than to apply poison to his legs, to take away their feeling; let them be gouty all they liked, so long as they were insensible of pain. God gives us leave enough to go when He is pleased to reduce us to a condition in which to live is far worse than to die. It is weakness to give in to infirmities, but it is madness to feed them. The Stoics say that to take one's leave of life, even at the height of prosperity, is living according to nature in a wise man, if he does it at the right moment — and in a fool it is to prolong life, though he be miserable, provided he is not in want of the things they reckon to be according to nature. As I do not break the law against thieves when I help myself to my own money and cut my own purse, nor that against arsonists when I burn my own wood, so I am not under the lash of laws against murderers for having deprived myself of my own life. Hegesias said that just as the condition of life did, so the condition of death ought to depend on our own choice. And Diogenes, meeting the philosopher Speusippus, so swollen with a chronic dropsy that he had to be carried in a litter, and greeted by him with the polite "I wish you good health," replied, "No health to you, who are content to live in such a condition."
And in fact, not long afterwards, Speusippus, weary of so languishing a life, found a means to die.

But this does not pass without dispute. Many are of opinion that we cannot quit this garrison of the world without the express command of Him who placed us in it; and that it is for God, who has placed us here, not just for ourselves but for His glory and the service of others, to dismiss us when it best pleases Him, and not for us to depart without His leave; that we are not born only for ourselves but for our country also, the laws of which require an account from us for the sake of their own interest and have an action of manslaughter against us; and that if these fail to take cognisance of the act, we are punished in the other world as deserters of our duty:
"Proxima deinde tenent maesti loca, qui sibi letum Insontes peperere manu, lucemque perosi Proiecere animas."
["In the next region the sad ones dwell, who, though free from guilt, slew themselves by their own hand and, hating the light, cast away their lives." — Aeneid, vi. 434.]

There is more constancy in bearing the chain we are tied to than in breaking it, and more telling evidence of fortitude in Regulus than in Cato; it is indiscretion and impatience that push us to these precipices. No misfortune can make true virtue turn her back; she seeks and demands evils, pains, and griefs, as the things by which she is nourished and sustained. The threats of tyrants, racks, and tortures serve only to rouse and quicken her:
"Duris ut ilex tonsa bipennibus Nigrae feraci frondis in Algido, Per damma, percmdes, ab ipso Ducit opes, animumque ferro."
["As on Mount Algidus, the sturdy oak draws fresh vigour and spirit from the very axe that prunes it." — Horace, Od., iv. 4, 57.]
And as another says:
"Non est, ut putas, virtus, pater, Timere vitam; sed malis ingentibus Obstare, nec se vertere, ac retro dare."
["Father, it is not virtue, as you suppose, to fear life, but to stand up to great misfortunes, not to turn and run from them." — Seneca, Thebais, i. 190.]
Or as this:
"Rebus in adversis facile est contemnere mortem Fortius ille facit, qui miser esse potest."
["In adversity it is easy to despise death; he acts more bravely who can endure being wretched." — Martial, xi. 56, 15.]
It is cowardice, not virtue, to lie crouched in a furrow under a tomb to dodge the blows of fortune. Virtue never stops, never strays from her path, for the greatest storm that blows:
"Si fractus illabatur orbis, Impavidum ferient ruinae."
["Should the world's axis crack, the ruins will only crush a fearless head." — Horace, Od., iii. 3, 7.]
More often, fleeing other troubles brings us to this one; in trying to dodge death, we often run straight into its jaws:
"Hic, rogo, non furor est, ne moriare, mori?"
["Tell me, is it not madness to die for fear of dying?" — Martial, ii. 80, 2.]
— like those who, for fear of a precipice, throw themselves headlong into it:
"Multos in summa pericula misfit Venturi timor ipse mali: fortissimus ille est, Qui promptus metuenda pati, si cominus instent, Et differre potest."
["The fear of future evils often drives men into extreme danger; he is truly brave who boldly faces the troubles he dreads, when they confront him and can be put off." — Lucan, vii. 104.]
"Usque adeo, mortis formidine, vitae Percipit humanos odium, lucisque videndae, Ut sibi consciscant moerenti pectore lethum Obliti fontem curarum hunc esse timorem."

["So far does dread of death produce in some men a hatred of life and of seeing the light that they kill themselves with grieving hearts, forgetting that this very fear is the source of their cares." — Lucretius, iii. 79.]

Plato, in his Laws, assigns an ignominious burial to the man who has deprived his nearest and best friend — namely himself — of life and his allotted course, not being compelled to do so by public judgment, by any sad and inescapable accident of fortune, nor by any unbearable disgrace, but merely driven on by cowardice and the feebleness of a fearful soul. And the opinion that makes so little of life is ridiculous, for it is our being — it is all we have. Things of a higher and more elevated existence may, indeed, look down on ours, but it is against nature for us to despise and discount ourselves. It is a disease peculiar to man, not found in any other creature, to hate and despise itself. And it is a vanity of the same kind to want to be something other than we are; the effect of such a wish does not even touch us, since it is contradicted and frustrated in itself. He who asks to be turned from a man into an angel does nothing for himself; he would be no better off for it, since, being no more, who would there be left to rejoice or be aware of this benefit on his behalf?
"Debet enim, misere cui forti, aegreque futurum est, Ipse quoque esse in eo turn tempore, cum male possit Accidere."
["For the man who is to suffer misery and pain in the future must himself still exist at the time when these ills are to befall him." — Lucretius, ibid., 874.]

Security, indolence, freedom from feeling, the absence of the ills of this life — which we pretend to buy at the price of dying — are no advantage to us. The man who escapes war to no purpose, if he cannot enjoy peace, and just as little to the purpose, the man who escapes trouble who cannot enjoy rest.

Among those of the first of these two opinions, there has been great debate as to what occasions are sufficient to justify deliberate self-murder, which they call "a reasonable exit." For though they say that men must sometimes die for trivial causes, since those that detain us in life are of no great weight either, yet there must be some limit. There are fantastic and senseless impulses that have driven not only individual men but whole nations to destroy themselves, of which I have given examples elsewhere. We also read of the Milesian virgins, who by a mad compact hanged themselves one after another until the magistrate took order in it, decreeing that the bodies of any found so hanged should be drawn naked through the city by the same halter. When Therykion tried to persuade Cleomenes to dispatch himself because of the ill posture of his affairs and, having missed a more honourable death in the lost battle, to accept this second-best one rather than give the conquerors leisure to inflict on him either a shameful death or a degrading life, Cleomenes, with a courage truly Stoic and Lacedaemonian, rejected his advice as unmanly and base: "That," he said, "is a remedy that will never be unavailable, but one a man should not resort to while an inch of hope remains." He told him that it was sometimes constancy and valour to live; that he wanted even his death to be of use to his country, and would make of it an act of honour and virtue. Therykion, nevertheless, thought himself in the right and did his own business; and Cleomenes did the same afterwards, but only after he had first tried out the utmost malice of fortune. Not all the troubles in the world are weighty enough to make a man die to dodge them; and besides, there are so many sudden and unexpected changes in human affairs that it is hard to judge rightly when we are at the end of our hope:
"Sperat et in saeva victus gladiator arena, Sit licet infesto pollice turba minax."
["Even the conquered gladiator in the cruel arena still hopes, though the threatening crowd, with thumb turned down, orders him to die." — Pentadius, De Spe, in Virgilii Catalecta.]

All things, says an old adage, are to be hoped for by a man while he lives. Yes — but, replies Seneca, why should it run more in a man's head that fortune can do all things for the living man, than this: that fortune has no power over the man who knows how to die? Josephus, engaged in such near and obvious danger, with a whole people violently set against him and no visible means of escape, was, as he himself tells us, advised by one of his friends in this extremity to dispatch himself. It was well for him that he still kept up hope, for fortune diverted the danger beyond all human expectation, and he saw himself delivered without any harm. Whereas Brutus and Cassius, on the contrary, threw away the last remains of Roman liberty, of which they were the sole protectors, by the haste and rashness with which they killed themselves before the proper time and a just occasion. Monsieur d'Anguien, at the battle of Cerisoles, twice tried to run himself through, despairing of the day, which was going very badly on that side of the field where he was engaged, and by that haste came very close to depriving himself of the enjoyment of so brave a victory. I have seen a hundred hares escape from the very teeth of the greyhounds:
"Aliquis carnifici suo superstes fuit."
["Some men have outlived their executioner." — Seneca, Ep., 13.]
"Multa dies, variusque labor mutabilis nevi Rettulit in melius; multos alterna revisens Lusit, et in solido rursus fortuna locavit."

["Length of days, and the changing labour of fickle time, have brought things back to a better state; fortune, returning by turns, has toyed with many and set them again on firm ground." — Aeneid, xi. 425.]
Pliny says there are only three sorts of diseases that give a man fair title to destroy himself; the worst of which is the stone in the bladder, when the urine is blocked.

[In the 1588 quarto edition of these essays, Pliny is said to mention two more — a pain in the stomach and a headache — which, he says (lib. xxv. c. 9), were almost the only three diseases for which men killed themselves.]

Seneca says only those which keep on disturbing the functions of the soul for a long time. And there have been some who, to avoid a worse death, have chosen one of their own liking. Democritus, general of the Aetolians, brought as a prisoner to Rome, found a way to escape by night; but, hotly pursued by his keepers, he fell on his own sword and died rather than let himself be retaken. Antinous and Theodotus, when their city of Epirus was reduced by the Romans to the last extremity, advised the people to kill themselves universally. The people preferring to give themselves up to the enemy, the two chiefs went to seek the death they wanted, rushing furiously upon the enemy with intent to strike home but not to ward off any blow.
