When the Island of Gozzo was taken some years ago by the Turks, a Sicilian who had two beautiful marriageable daughters killed them both with his own hand, along with their mother who ran in to save them; that done, he sallied out of the house with a crossbow and arquebus, killed with two shots the two Turks nearest his door, and drawing his sword charged furiously among the rest, where he was quickly surrounded and cut to pieces — by that means delivering his family and himself from slavery and dishonour. The Jewish women, after circumcising their children, threw them and themselves down a precipice to escape the cruelty of Antigonus. I have been told of a man of rank in one of our prisons whose friends, hearing that he would certainly be condemned, suborned a priest to tell him — to spare him the disgrace of such a death — that the only means of his deliverance was to commend himself to such-and-such a saint under such-and-such vows, and to fast eight days together without taking any nourishment, whatever weakness or faintness he might feel. He followed their advice, and so destroyed himself before he was aware, not suspecting death or any danger in the experiment. Scribonia, advising her nephew Libo to kill himself rather than wait for the stroke of justice, told him that to keep his life only to put it after into the hands of those who within three or four days would haul him to execution was to do other people's business, and that to keep his blood for them to gratify their malice was to serve his enemies.

We read in the Bible that Nicanor, the persecutor of the law of God, having sent his soldiers to seize the good old man Razis — surnamed, for his virtue, the father of the Jews — the good man, seeing no other remedy, his gates burned down and the enemies ready to take him, chose to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of his wicked adversaries and let himself be cruelly butchered by them, contrary to the honour of his rank. He stabbed himself with his own sword, but in haste the blow had not gone home; so he ran and threw himself headlong from the top of a wall on the men below. They moved apart and made room, and he landed straight on his head. Yet, feeling still in himself some remains of life, he renewed his courage, sprang up on his feet all bloody and wounded, and making his way through the crowd to a steep rock, drew out his bowels through one of his wounds and, tearing and pulling them apart with both hands, threw them among his pursuers, all the while calling on divine vengeance for their cruelty and injustice.

Of violations of the conscience, that against the chastity of a woman is, in my opinion, the most to be avoided, since there is a certain pleasure naturally mixed with it, and for that reason her refusal cannot be perfectly complete — so that the violence seems mixed with some small consent on the part of the forced. Church history has several examples of devout persons who embraced death to secure themselves from outrages prepared by tyrants against their religion and honour. Pelagia and Sophronia, both canonised: the first threw herself with her mother and sisters into the river to avoid being forced by some soldiers; the second killed herself to avoid being raped by the Emperor Maxentius.

It may, perhaps, be an honour to us in future ages that a learned author of our day, a Parisian, has gone to great pains to persuade the ladies of our time to take any other course rather than fall into so awful a meditation as that despair. I am sorry he had never heard, that he might have included it among his other stories, the saying of a woman that was told to me at Toulouse, who had passed through the hands of some soldiers: "God be praised," she said, "that at least once in my life I have had my fill without sin." In truth, these cruelties are very unworthy of the French good nature, and, God be thanked, our air is well purged of them since this good advice came in: it is enough that they say "no" while doing it, according to the rule of the good Marot.
"Un doulx nenny, avec un doulx sourire Est tant honneste." — Marot.

History is everywhere full of people who, by a thousand routes, have exchanged a painful and tedious life for death. Lucius Aruntius killed himself, he said, to flee both the future and the past. Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus, after being pardoned by Nero, killed themselves — either disdaining to live by the favour of so wicked a man, or so as not to be troubled at some other time to seek a second pardon, given the readiness of his nature to suspect and credit accusations against worthy men. Spargapises, son of Queen Tomyris, taken prisoner of war by Cyrus, used the first favour Cyrus showed him — ordering him untied — to kill himself, claiming no other benefit of liberty than to be revenged upon himself for the disgrace of having been captured. Boges, governor of Eion for King Xerxes, besieged by the Athenian army under Cimon, refused the terms offered (a safe return into Asia with all his wealth), unable to bear surviving the loss of a post his master had given him to keep. So, after defending the city to the last extremity, when nothing was left to eat, he first threw all the gold and everything else the enemy could plunder into the river Strymon, then ordered a great pyre lit and the throats cut of all the women, children, concubines, and servants, whose bodies he threw into the fire, and at last leaped into it himself.

Ninachetuen, an Indian lord, at the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to strip him, with no clear cause, of his command in Malacca, in order to transfer it to the King of Campar, took this resolution: he had a scaffold built, longer than broad, supported by columns royally hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers and abundant perfumes; and when all was ready, he came out into the street in a robe of cloth of gold studded with jewels of great value, and mounted the steps to the scaffold, at one corner of which he had a pyre of aromatic wood lit. Everyone ran to see what these unusual preparations were for; whereupon Ninachetuen, with a manly but indignant air, set out how much he had served the Portuguese nation, and with how unspotted fidelity he had behaved in his charge; that, having so often, sword in hand, shown for others that honour was much dearer to him than life, he was not to abandon care for it on his own behalf; that, since fortune denied him any way of resisting the affront prepared for him, his courage at least required him to free himself from the feeling of it, and not to become a tale told by the people or a triumph to men less deserving than himself. Having said this, he leaped into the fire.

Sextilia, wife of Scaurus, and Paxaea, wife of Labeo, to encourage their husbands to escape the dangers pressing upon them — in which they had no share but conjugal affection — voluntarily sacrificed their own lives to serve them in this extreme necessity for company and example. What they did for their husbands, Cocceius Nerva did for his country, with less utility though with equal devotion: this great lawyer, flourishing in health, wealth, reputation, and favour with the emperor, had no other reason to kill himself but the bare pity of the miserable state of the Roman Republic. Nothing can be added to the beauty of the death of the wife of Fulvius, a familiar favourite of Augustus. Augustus, having discovered that he had divulged an important secret entrusted to him, received him very coldly one morning when he came to court and looked grimly at him. Fulvius returned home in despair and told his wife sorrowfully that, having fallen into this misfortune, he was resolved to kill himself; to which she answered roundly, "It is only right that you should, since after so often experiencing the looseness of my tongue you would not take warning. But let me kill myself first" — and without saying more she ran herself through the body with a sword. Vibius Virrius, despairing of the safety of his city, besieged by the Romans, and of their mercy, in the last debate of his city's senate, after many arguments to the same end, concluded that the noblest way to escape fortune was by their own hands. He told them the enemy would have them in honour, and Hannibal would feel how many faithful friends he had abandoned, and invited those who approved his advice to come to a good supper he had ready at home, where, after they had eaten well, they would all drink together of what he had prepared — "a drink," he said, "that will deliver our bodies from torments, our souls from insult, and our eyes and ears from feeling the many hateful evils the conquered suffer from cruel and implacable conquerors." He said he had arranged for proper persons to throw their bodies on a funeral pyre before his door as soon as they were dead. Many approved this high resolution, but few imitated it. Twenty-seven senators followed him, who, after having tried to drown the thought of this fatal decision in wine, ended the feast with the deadly mess; and embracing one another, after lamenting together their country's misfortune, some withdrew home to their own houses, others stayed to be burned with Vibius on his funeral pyre. All were so long in dying — the vapour of the wine having clogged the veins and so deferred the effect of the poison — that some of them came within an hour of seeing the enemy inside the walls of Capua, which was taken the next morning, and of undergoing the miseries they had at so dear a rate tried to avoid. Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Alexander, besieging a city of the Indies, those within, finding themselves very hard pressed, took a vigorous resolve to deny him the pleasure of his victory: they burned themselves, with the whole city, in defiance of his clemency — a new sort of war, where the enemies sought to save them, and they to destroy themselves, doing as much to make themselves sure of death as men do to secure life.

Astapa, a city of Spain, finding itself too weak in walls and defenders to withstand the Romans, the inhabitants made a heap of all their riches and furniture in the public square; and having ranged on this heap all the women and children, piled wood and other combustible matter around them to set them quickly on fire, and left fifty of their young men to carry out what they had resolved, they made a desperate sally where, for lack of strength to win, they got themselves all killed. The fifty, after massacring every living soul in the whole city and putting fire to the pile, threw themselves last into it, ending their generous freedom in an unfeeling rather than a sorrowful and shameful manner, giving the enemy to understand that, had fortune so pleased, they had as much courage to snatch victory from them as to frustrate it and render it dreadful — even mortal to those who, lured by the gleam of the gold melting in this flame, came too close: many were suffocated and burned there, kept from retreating by the crowd that pressed in behind.

The Abydeans, when pressed by King Philip, took the same resolve, but, lacking time, could not carry it out. The king, struck with horror at the rash haste of this resolution (the treasure and movables they had condemned to the flames being first secured), withdrew his soldiers and gave them three days to kill themselves in, that they might do it with more order and at greater ease — a time which they filled with blood and slaughter beyond the utmost excess of any hostile cruelty, so that not one soul was left alive that had any power to destroy itself. There are countless examples of such mass resolutions, which seem the fiercer and crueler the more universal the effect, and yet are really less so than when carried out by individuals: what argument and persuasion cannot do with single men, they can do with all, the ardour of society overriding individual judgments.

The condemned who, in the reign of Tiberius, lived to be executed, forfeited their goods and were denied burial rites; those who anticipated execution by killing themselves were buried, and were free to dispose of their estates by will.

But men sometimes covet death out of hope of a greater good. "I desire," says St. Paul, "to be with Christ," and "who shall rid me of these bands?" Cleombrotus of Ambracia, after reading Plato's Phaedo, conceived so great a desire for the life to come that, without any other occasion, he threw himself into the sea. By which it appears how improperly we call this voluntary dissolution despair — to which the eagerness of hope often inclines us, and sometimes a calm and tempered desire arising from a mature and deliberate judgment. Jacques du Chastel, bishop of Soissons, on St. Louis's foreign expedition, seeing the king and whole army about to return to France, leaving the cause of religion unfinished, took the resolve to go straight to Paradise instead. So, having taken a solemn farewell of his friends, he charged alone, in the sight of everyone, into the enemy's army, where he was at once cut to pieces. In a certain kingdom of the newly discovered world, on a day of solemn procession when the idol they worship is drawn in public on a chariot of marvellous size, besides the many seen cutting off pieces of their flesh to offer to it, there are others who throw themselves down in its path, to be crushed and broken to pieces under the heavy wheels, to obtain after death the veneration of sanctity — which is duly paid them. The death of the bishop, sword in hand, has more magnanimity in it and less sensation, since the heat of battle takes away part of the latter.

There are some governments that have taken it upon themselves to regulate the justice and the proper occasion of voluntary death. Formerly, in our city of Marseilles, a poison prepared from hemlock was kept at the public expense for those who wished to hasten their end, after first laying out before the six hundred (who were their senate) the reasons and motives of their design. It was not lawful otherwise — only by leave from the magistrate, and on just occasion, could a man do violence to himself. The same law was in use in other places too.

Sextus Pompeius, on his way to Asia, called at the isle of Cea in Negropont. It happened, while he was there — as we have it from one who was with him — that a woman of great quality, having explained to her fellow citizens why she was resolved to put an end to her life, invited Pompeius to her death to render it more honourable; an invitation he accepted. After long trying in vain with the great power of his eloquence and persuasion to turn her from her purpose, he gave way in the end to her own will. She had passed the age of ninety in a very happy state of body and mind. Lying on her bed, dressed better than usual and leaning on her elbow, "The gods," she said, "O Sextus Pompeius — and rather those I leave than those I go to seek — reward you, that you have not disdained to be both the counsellor of my life and the witness of my death. For my part, having always known the smiles of fortune, for fear that the desire of living too long may make me see a contrary face, I am going, by a happy end, to dismiss the rest of my soul, leaving behind two daughters of my body and a legion of grandchildren." Having said this, with some exhortations to her family to live in peace, she divided her goods among them, commended her household gods to her eldest daughter, and boldly took the cup that held the poison. After making her vows and prayers to Mercury to conduct her to some happy abode in the other world, she briskly swallowed the deadly draught. This done, she entertained the company with a running account of its progress and how the cold gradually seized the several parts of her body one after another; until, having at last told them it was beginning to seize on her heart and bowels, she called her daughters to do the last office and close her eyes.

Pliny tells us of a certain Hyperborean nation where, owing to the gentle temperature of the air, lives rarely end except by the voluntary surrender of the inhabitants, who, weary of and satiated with living, have the custom, at a very old age, after a good meal, of throwing themselves into the sea from the top of a certain rock set aside for that purpose. Pain and the fear of a worse death seem to me the most excusable of all incitements.

title: To-morrow's a new day
paragraphs: I give, as it seems to me, with good reason the palm to Jacques Amyot above all our French writers — not only for the simplicity and purity of his language, in which he excels all others, nor for his perseverance in carrying through so long a work, nor for the depth of his learning that allowed him to smooth out and untangle so knotty and intricate an author so successfully (for whatever people say, I know nothing of Greek; but I meet with a sense so well held together and sustained throughout his whole translation that he must either have known the true mind of the author, or, by long acquaintance with him, imprinted a vivid and general idea of Plutarch in his soul — for he has given us nothing that detracts from or contradicts him); but above all I am most taken with him for having so well chosen a book so worthy and so useful to present to his country. We ignorant fellows would have been lost if this book had not raised us out of the dirt; by his favour we now dare speak and write; the ladies are able to instruct schoolmasters; it is our breviary. If this good man is still alive, I would commend Xenophon to him to do as much for that author; it is a much easier task than the other, and consequently fitter for his age. And besides, though I cannot say quite how, it seems to me he trips briskly and clearly enough over steps another would have stumbled at, yet still his style seems more his own where he does not meet those difficulties, and rolls along at his ease.

I was just now reading the passage where Plutarch says of himself that Rusticus, being present at a declamation of his in Rome, received a packet from the emperor and put off opening it until everything was over — for which, he says, the whole company highly praised that man's gravity. True enough, given that he was on the subject of curiosity and that eager passion for news which makes us, with so much indiscretion and impatience, drop everything to attend to a newcomer and tear open on the spot, no matter what company we are in, the letters delivered to us — he had reason to applaud Rusticus's gravity in this instance, and he might further have added the commendation of his civility and courtesy in not interrupting the flow of his declamation. But I doubt whether anyone can commend his prudence: with unexpected letters, especially from an emperor, putting off reading them might have done great harm. The vice opposite to curiosity is negligence, to which I naturally incline, and in which I have seen some men so extreme that one might find letters sent them three or four days before still sealed in their pockets.

I never open any letters addressed to another — not only those entrusted to me, but even those that fortune has steered into my hand. I am cross with myself if my eyes unintentionally pick up any contents from letters of importance that a great man is reading while I stand near him. Never was a man less inquisitive or less prying into other men's affairs than I.

In our fathers' time, Monsieur de Boutières nearly lost Turin by having, while in good company at supper, put off reading information sent to him of the treason plotted against that city, which he commanded. And this same Plutarch has informed me that Julius Caesar would have saved himself if, on his way to the Senate the day he was assassinated by the conspirators, he had read a note handed to him on the way. He also tells the story of Archias, the tyrant of Thebes, who, the night before the design Pelopidas had plotted to kill him and restore his country to liberty was executed, was sent a full written account of the whole conspiracy by another Archias, an Athenian; and this packet having been delivered to him while he sat at supper, he put off opening it, saying — what afterwards became a proverb in Greece — "Business tomorrow."

A wise man may, I think, out of consideration for another — so as not to disturb the company, as Rusticus did, or break off some important business in hand — defer reading or hearing some new thing brought to him; but to defer for his own interest or private pleasure, especially if he is a public minister, refusing to interrupt his dinner or break his sleep, is inexcusable. There was anciently at Rome the so-called "consular place" at the table, which was the most honourable as being the freest, and most accessible to those who came in to speak with the person seated there. From which it appears that, even at meals, they did not entirely abandon the concern of other affairs and incidents. But when all is said, it is very hard in human actions to give so exact a rule on moral grounds that fortune will not still maintain her own right within it.

title: Of conscience
paragraphs: The Sieur de la Brousse, my brother, and I, travelling one day together during the time of our civil wars, met a gentleman of good standing. He was of the opposite party, though I did not know it, for he pretended otherwise. The trouble in this kind of war is that the cards are so shuffled — your enemy not distinguished from yourself by any obvious mark of language or dress, having been raised under the same laws, climate, and manners — that it is very hard to avoid confusion and disorder. This made me afraid of meeting any of our own troops in a place where I was not known, that I might not be in fear to tell my name, and perhaps worse — as had happened to me before, when by such a mistake I lost both men and horses, including an Italian gentleman, my page, whom I had bred with the greatest care and affection, in whom a youth of great promise was wretchedly extinguished. But the gentleman my brother and I met had so desperate, half-dead a fear of meeting any horsemen or passing by any of the towns that held for the King, that I at last realised it was the alarm of conscience. The poor man felt as if through his visor and the crosses on his cassock one might have seen into his bosom and read the most secret intentions of his heart — so wonderful is the power of conscience. It makes us betray, accuse, and fight against ourselves, and for want of other witnesses, give evidence against ourselves:
"Occultum quatiens animo tortore flagellum."
["The torturer of the soul brandishing a hidden lash within." — Juvenal, iii. 195.]

This story is in every child's mouth: Bessus the Paeonian, reproached for wantonly pulling down a nest of young sparrows and killing them, replied that he had reason to do so, since those little birds never ceased falsely accusing him of the murder of his father. The parricide had until then been concealed and unknown, but the avenging fury of conscience caused it to be revealed by the very man who was to suffer for it. Hesiod corrects Plato's saying that punishment closely follows sin: it is, he says, born at the same moment as the sin. Whoever expects punishment already suffers it, and whoever has deserved it expects it. Wickedness contrives torments against itself:
"Malum consilium consultori pessimum."
["Bad counsel is worst for the counsellor." — in Aulus Gellius, iv. 5.]
— as the wasp stings and hurts another but most of all itself, since it loses its sting and its use forever there:
"Vitasque in vulnere ponunt."
["And leave their own lives in the wound." — Virgil, Georg., iv. 238.]

The cantharides carry about them, by a quirk of nature, an antidote to their own poison. In the same way, at the very moment when men take delight in vice, there springs in the conscience a discomfort that torments us sleeping and waking with various distressing fancies:
"Quippe ubi se multi, per somnia saepe loquentes, Aut morbo delirantes, protraxe ferantur, Et celata diu in medium peccata dedisse."
["Surely many men, often talking in their sleep or raving in disease, are said to have betrayed themselves and brought to light offences long concealed." — Lucretius, v. 1157.]

Apollodorus dreamed that he saw himself flayed by the Scythians and then boiled in a cauldron, and that his heart muttered these words: "I am the cause of all these miseries that have come on you." Epicurus said that no hiding-place could conceal the wicked, since they could never be sure of being hidden while their conscience exposed them to themselves.
"Prima est haec ultio, quod se Judice nemo nocens absolvitur."
["This is the first punishment of guilt: that no guilty man is acquitted in his own court." — Juvenal, xiii. 2.]

As a bad conscience fills us with fear, so a good one gives us greater confidence and assurance; and I can truly say that I have gone through several dangers with a steadier step because of the secret knowledge I had of my own will and the innocence of my intentions:
"Conscia mens ut cuique sua est, ita concipit intra Pectora pro facto spemque metumque suo."
["As each man's conscience is, so within his breast he conceives hope or fear, according to his deed." — Ovid, Fast., i. 485.]

There are a thousand examples of this; but three of one and the same person will be enough. Scipio, being accused one day before the people of Rome of crimes of a very high nature, instead of excusing himself or flattering his judges, said, "It will be a fine thing for you to sit in judgment on a head by whose means you have the power to judge all the world." Another time, to a string of impeachments brought against him by a tribune of the people, instead of making his defence he said, "Let us go, citizens — let us go and give thanks to the gods for the victory they gave me over the Carthaginians on this day," and walking off ahead toward the temple, he had presently the whole assembly, and his accuser himself, following at his heels. And when Petilius, put up to it by Cato, demanded an account of the money that had passed through his hands in the province of Antioch, Scipio, coming into the senate for that purpose, produced from under his robe a book in which, he told them, was an exact account of his receipts and disbursements; but when he was asked to hand it over to the prothonotary for examination, he refused, saying he would not do himself so great a disgrace, and in the presence of the whole senate tore the book in pieces with his own hands. I do not believe that the most calloused conscience could have counterfeited so great an assurance. He had naturally too high a spirit and was used to too high a fortune, says Titus Livius, to know how to be guilty, and to lower himself to the meanness of defending his innocence. The putting of men to the rack is a dangerous invention, and seems to be more a trial of patience than of truth. Both the man who has the fortitude to endure it conceals the truth, and the man who has not — for why should pain sooner make me confess what is, than force me to say what is not? And on the other hand, if the man who is not guilty of what he is accused of has the courage to undergo those torments, why should not the guilty man have the same, when so fair a reward as life is in his sights? I believe the basis of this invention comes from considering the force of conscience: for in the guilty man it seems to assist the rack in making him confess his fault and shake his resolution; and in the innocent it fortifies him against the torture. But, all said, it is in plain truth a trial full of uncertainty and danger. What would not a man say, what would not a man do, to avoid such unbearable torments?
"Etiam innocentes cogit mentiri dolor."
["Pain will make even the innocent lie." — Publius Syrus, De Dolore.]

From which it comes that he whom the judge has racked in order not to put him to death innocent, ends by being put to death both innocent and racked. A thousand and a thousand have charged their own heads by false confessions — among whom I count Philotas, considering the circumstances of the trial Alexander put him to and the course of his torture. But, so it goes, some say it is the least evil human weakness could invent. Very inhumanly, even so, and to very little purpose, in my opinion.

Many nations, less barbarous in this than the Greeks and Romans who call them so, hold it horrible and cruel to torment and tear a man to pieces for a fault of which they are still in doubt. How can he help your ignorance? Are you not unjust who, to avoid killing him without cause, do worse than kill him? And to prove this, just observe how often men prefer to die without reason rather than undergo this examination, more painful than the execution itself, and which often anticipates execution by its very extremity and carries it out. I do not know where I got this story, but it exactly matches the conscience of our justice in this regard. A countrywoman accused, before a general of very severe discipline, one of his soldiers of having taken from her children the little bit of broth she had left to feed them with, the army having consumed all the rest; but there was no proof of it. The general, having warned the woman to be very careful what she said, for that she would make herself guilty of a false accusation if she lied, and she sticking to her story, he at once had the soldier's belly slit open to find out the truth of the fact — and the woman was found to be right. An instructive sentence.

title: Use makes perfect
paragraphs: It cannot be expected that argument and instruction, however willingly we surrender our belief to what we read, will carry us far enough to act on it, unless we also train and shape the soul by experience for the course we have designed it for. Otherwise, when the moment comes, it will find itself at a loss. That is why the philosophers most ambitious of excellence were not content to sit at home in retirement and ease, waiting for fortune to spring on them while they were raw and untried. They went out to meet her, deliberately throwing themselves into the proof of difficulties. Some gave up their wealth to practise a voluntary poverty; others sought out labour and a harsh way of life to harden themselves against hardship and inconvenience; others deprived themselves of their dearest organs, such as sight or the instruments of generation, lest a pleasure too sweet and too easy should soften and corrupt the steadiness of the soul.

But in dying, which is the greatest task we have to do, practice can give us no help at all. A man can fortify himself by habit against pain, shame, want, and other such accidents, but death is something we can only experiment with once, and we are all apprentices when we come to it. There have been men in antiquity who managed their time so well that they tried in death itself to taste and savour it, bending the full force of their minds to discover what this passage is; but none of them has come back to tell us the news:
"Nemo expergitus exstat, Frigida quem semel est vitai pausa sequuta."
["No one wakes again once the cold pause of life has overtaken him." — Lucretius, iii. 942]

Julius Canus, a noble Roman of rare constancy and virtue, had been condemned to death by that worthless creature Caligula. Among the many remarkable proofs he gave of his resolve, just as he was about to receive the executioner's stroke, a philosopher friend of his asked him: "Well, Canus, where is your soul now? What is she doing? What are you thinking of?" — "I was thinking," he answered, "of how to hold myself ready, with my faculties settled and fixed, to see whether in this short, quick instant of death I could catch the motion of the soul as she leaves the body, and whether she feels anything in the parting; so that, if I could, I might come back afterwards and report it to my friends." This man philosophises not just up to death but in death itself. What an extraordinary self-possession, what bravery of mind, to want his own death to be a lesson to him, and to have the leisure to think of other matters in such a moment:
"Jus hoc animi morientis habebat."
["He had this mighty power of mind even in dying." — Lucan, viii. 636.]

And yet I fancy there is a certain way of making death familiar to us, and of testing in some sort what it is. We can gain an experience of it which, if not complete and perfect, will at least not be useless, and may render us steadier and more assured. If we cannot overtake it, we may approach it and look at it; if we cannot reach the fort itself, we may at least scout the approaches. It is no accident that we are taught to consider sleep as a likeness of death. How easily do we pass from waking into sleep; with how little concern do we lose the knowledge of light and of ourselves. The capacity to sleep might seem useless and contrary to nature, since it strips us of all action and feeling — were it not that by sleep nature is teaching us that she has made us as much for dying as for living, and in the middle of life shows us the eternal state she has in store for us afterwards, to accustom us to it and take away our fear. But people who, by some violent accident, have fallen into a faint and lost all sense have, I think, come very near seeing the true and natural face of death. The moment of passage itself, in fact, is not to be feared for any pain or distress it brings, since feeling requires time, and the moment of death is so short and abrupt that it must be insensible. It is the approaches we have to fear, and those do fall within the range of experience.

Many things look larger in imagination than they turn out to be in fact. I have spent a good part of my life in perfect health — not just sound, but sprightly and full of vigour — and this state, so green and lively, made the idea of sickness terrifying to me; when I came actually to experience illness, I found the attacks faint and easy compared with what I had feared. I see it every day. If I am sheltered in a warm room on a stormy and tempestuous night, I wonder how anyone can live out of doors, and feel sorry for those caught in the fields; if I am out there myself, I have no wish to be anywhere else. Being shut up in a room I always imagined unbearable; but I was quickly inured to a week, then a month, of being so confined, in a weak, ailing, and dejected condition. And I have found that, in times of health, I felt much more pity for the sick than I now feel deserves to be felt for me when I am one. The force of imagination heightens nearly half the substance and reality of the thing. I hope that when I come to die I will find the same; that, when all is said, the trouble I take, the preparation and assistance I call in to face the blow, is more than the case warrants. Still, we cannot give ourselves too much advantage.

During the time of our third or second civil troubles (I do not quite remember which), I went out one day to take the air about a league from my house, which sits at the very centre of all the violence and mischief of the recent French civil wars. Thinking myself perfectly safe and so close to home that I had no need of better equipment, I had taken a horse with a comfortable pace but not much strength. On my way back, an occasion suddenly arose to use this horse for something he was not used to, and one of my retinue — a tall, hefty fellow on a strong German horse with a hard mouth, fresh and full of go — galloped up to play the brave and push ahead of the others, charging full speed in the very track I was on, crashing like a Colossus onto the small man and the small horse with such weight and momentum that he flipped us both over, heels in the air. The horse went down stunned by the fall; I lay stretched out ten or twelve paces beyond him, my face battered and broken, my sword (which had been in my hand) another ten paces further on, my belt smashed to pieces, with no more motion or sense than a log. That was the only swoon I have ever had in my life until that hour. Those with me, after trying every means they could to bring me round and concluding I was dead, picked me up in their arms and with great difficulty carried me home — about half a French league away. On the way, after I had been given up for dead for more than two hours, I began to stir and to draw breath. So much blood had pooled in my stomach that nature had to rouse her forces to discharge it. They set me on my feet, and I threw up a whole bucketful of clotted blood, as I did several more times along the road. This relieved me enough that I began to recover a little life, but so slowly and by such small steps that my first sensations were closer to the approaches of death than of life:
"Perche, dubbiosa ancor del suo ritorno, Non s'assicura attonita la mente."
["For the soul, still uncertain of its return, cannot in its stupor compose itself." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, xii. 74.]

The memory of this accident, which is firmly imprinted on my mind, presenting me so naturally with the image and idea of death, has in some way reconciled me to that grim adventure. When I first began to open my eyes, my sight was so confused, so weak, and so dim that I could distinguish nothing but the light:
"Come quel ch'or apre, or chiude Gli occhi, mezzo tra'l sonno e l'esser desto."
["Like a man who now opens, now closes his eyes, halfway between sleep and waking." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, viii. 26.]

As for the functions of the soul, they came back at the same pace and to the same degree as those of the body. I saw myself all bloody, my doublet stained from top to bottom with the blood I had vomited. The first thought that came into my head was that I had been shot through with a harquebuss, since a great many shots had been fired around us. It seemed to me that my life was just hanging on my lips, and I shut my eyes to help, as I thought, in pushing it out, taking pleasure in languishing and letting myself go. It was an impression that only skimmed the surface of my soul, as faint and weak as everything else, but really, far from being painful, it was mingled with the sweetness people feel when they slide into sleep.

I believe this is the very same state we see those people in who faint with weakness in the agony of death; we pity them without cause, supposing them tortured by sharp pains or that their souls are bearing painful thoughts. I have always held, against the common opinion and particularly against La Boétie, that those we see so subdued and stupefied at the approach of death, or overwhelmed by long illness, or felled by some sudden accident like a stroke or a fit of falling sickness,

"Vi morbi saepe coactus Ante oculos aliquis nostros, ut fulminis ictu, Concidit, et spumas agit; ingemit, et tremit artus; Desipit, extentat nervos, torquetur, anhelat, Inconstanter, et in jactando membra fatigat;"

["Often, struck down by the force of disease, someone falls before our eyes as if by a thunderbolt, foaming, groaning, his limbs trembling, his mind wandering, his sinews stretched, racked, gasping irregularly, wearing himself out in convulsions." — Lucretius, iii. 485.]

— or wounded in the head, whom we hear muttering and now and then groaning grievously — though we gather from these signs that they seem to retain some consciousness and that there are movements of the body — I have always believed, I say, that both body and soul are numbed and asleep,
"Vivit, et est vitae nescius ipse suae,"
["He lives, and does not know that he is alive." — Ovid, Tristia, i. 3, 12.]

and I could not believe that with so deep a stupefaction of the limbs and so great a failure of the senses, the soul could keep any power inwardly to take notice of herself; and therefore that they have no tormenting reflections to make them feel and consider the misery of their state, and consequently are not much to be pitied.

For my own part, I can imagine no state more unbearable and frightful than to have the soul lively and afflicted, with no way of expressing itself — like, say, men sent to execution with their tongues cut out first (except that, in this sort of dying, the most silent seems to me the most graceful, if accompanied by a grave and steady countenance); or like those wretched prisoners who fall into the hands of the brutal hangman-soldiers of our day, who torment them with every kind of inhuman treatment to force them to pay some impossible ransom, while keeping them, meanwhile, in a place and condition where they have no means of expressing or signalling their thoughts and misery. The poets imagined gods who favoured the deliverance of those undergoing a lingering death:
"Hunc ego Diti Sacrum jussa fero, teque isto corpore solvo."
["I, ordered to do it, bear this sacred thing as an offering to Pluto, and from that body release you." — Aeneid, iv. 782.]

Both the broken words and the short, irregular answers one sometimes gets out of such people by shouting and making a fuss around them, or the motions that seem to consent to what we want them to do, are no proof that they are alive in any full sense. The same thing happens to us, at the edge of sleep before it fully takes us, when we perceive as in a dream what is going on around us, and follow the last things being said with a confused and uncertain hearing that barely touches the borders of the soul, and we answer the last words spoken to us with replies that have more chance than sense in them.

Now, since I have actually tried it, I have no doubt that I have judged this rightly so far. For first of all, while I was in my swoon, I worked to rip open the buttons of my doublet with my nails — my sword was gone — and yet I felt nothing in my imagination that hurt me; for we have many movements in us that do not come from our direction:
"Semianimesque micant digiti, ferrumque retractant;"
["The half-dead fingers twitch, and grasp again at the sword." — Aeneid, x. 396.]
Likewise, people falling stretch out their arms before them by a natural impulse, which prompts our limbs to actions and motions without any orders from our reason.
"Falciferos memorant currus abscindere membra . . . Ut tremere in terra videatur ab artubus id quod Decidit abscissum; cum mens tamen atque hominis vis Mobilitate mali, non quit sentire dolorem."

["They tell of scythe-bearing chariots cutting off limbs, so that the severed limb is seen to quiver on the ground; and yet the mind of the man from whom it was cut, by the swiftness of the stroke, feels no pain." — Lucretius, iii. 642.]

My stomach was so loaded with the clotted blood that my hands moved to that part of their own accord, as they often do to a place that itches, without being directed by the will. There are several animals, and even human beings, in whom you can see the muscles twitch and quiver after they are dead. Everyone knows from experience that there are parts of us that stiffen or go limp without our permission. Now those passions which only touch the outer rind of us cannot really be called ours; for them to be ours, the whole man must take part, and the pains felt in the hand or the foot while we are asleep are none of ours.

As I drew near my house, where the news of my fall had already arrived ahead of me and my family had come out to meet me with the usual commotion, I not only made some short answer to their questions, but they tell me I was lucid enough to order them to bring a horse to my wife, whom I had seen on the road struggling and wearing herself out on the rough and hilly track. This would seem to come from a soul still doing its work, but it was nothing of the kind in me. I had no idea what I was saying or doing; these were idle clouds of thought stirred up by the sense-impressions of the eyes and ears, and they did not come from me. I did not know where I had come from or where I was going, nor was I able to weigh or take in what was said to me. They were only light effects produced by the senses out of habit; whatever the soul contributed was as in a dream, lightly grazed, licked, and dewed by the soft pressure of the senses. Even so, my condition was in truth very easy and quiet. I had no grief upon me, either for others or for myself; it was an extreme languor and weakness, without any kind of pain. I saw my own house but did not recognise it. When they had put me to bed I felt an indescribable sweetness in that rest; for I had been hauled and lugged about pitifully by those poor men, who had taken the trouble to carry me in their arms over a long and rough way and had several times worn themselves out in the process. They offered me various remedies, but I would take none, certain that I had been mortally wounded in the head. And in fact it would have been a very happy death: the weakness of my mind robbed me of the power of judging, and the weakness of my body of the power of feeling. I was letting myself slip away so sweetly, so gently, that I can hardly think of an action less troublesome than that was. But when I came back to myself and resumed my faculties:
"Ut tandem sensus convaluere mei,"
["When at last my lost senses recovered." — Ovid, Tristia, i. 3, 14.]

— which was two or three hours later — I suddenly felt myself in terrible pain, my limbs battered and bruised by the fall, and was so ill for two or three nights afterwards that I thought I was dying all over again, but a more painful death this time, having already taken myself for dead; and to this day I still feel the bruises of that terrible shock. I should not leave out that the last thing they could get into my head was the memory of the accident itself, and I had it told to me over and over — where I was going, where I had come from, what time of day the mishap had happened — before I could grasp it. As for the manner of my fall, that was hidden from me out of consideration for the man who had caused it, and other little stories were invented to cover it. But a long time afterwards, and the very next day on which my memory began to come back and to picture for me the state I was in at the instant I saw that horse driving full tilt at me (for I had glimpsed him at my heels and given myself up for gone, though the thought had been so sudden that fear had had no time to step in) — it seemed to me like a flash of lightning piercing my soul, and as if I had come back from the other world.

This long story about so slight an accident would seem pointless enough, were it not for what I have gained from it for my own use; for I really do find that to get acquainted with death there is no need to do more than approach it closely. Every man, as Pliny says, is a good teacher to himself, provided he is able to observe himself at close quarters. What I offer here is not a doctrine, it is my study; not someone else's lesson, but my own; and if I share it, that should not be taken badly, since what is useful to me may, perhaps, also be useful to another. As for the rest, I spoil nothing; I use nothing but my own. If I play the fool, it is at my own expense and nobody else's; it is a folly that will die with me, and that no one is going to inherit. We hear of only two or three of the ancients who walked this path, and even there I cannot say whether they did it in the same way, since I know nothing of them but their names. No one since has followed the track. It is a rough road, rougher than it looks, to follow a soul as wandering and uncertain as ours; to push into the dark depths of its tangled inner windings; to choose and seize so many small nimble motions. It is a new and unusual undertaking, and it draws us away from the common and most respected occupations of the world. For many years now my thoughts have had no other aim or focus than myself, and I have pried into and studied nothing but myself; or if I study anything else, it is to apply it to myself, or rather inside myself. And yet I do not think it a fault if, like other people who do the same with much less profitable subjects, I share what I have learned in this one, even though I am not very pleased with my own progress. There is no description so difficult, nor surely so useful, as that of oneself; and even there a man has to curl his hair and dress up to appear in public — and I am perpetually grooming myself, because I am eternally on my own description. Custom has made it improper to speak about oneself, and forbids it outright, out of hatred for the boasting that seems inseparable from any testimony men give about themselves:
"In vitium ducit culpae fuga."
["The avoidance of a mere fault often leads us into a greater one." Or: "The escape from a fault leads into a vice." — Horace, Ars Poetica, line 31.]

This is, instead of blowing the child's nose, cutting it off altogether. I think the cure is worse than the disease. But granting that it must be sheer presumption to entertain people with talk about oneself, still, pursuing my general design, I cannot refrain from an action that publishes this weakness of mine, nor conceal a fault which I not only practise but profess. To speak my mind freely, however, I think that the habit of condemning wine because some people get drunk on it is itself to be condemned; we can only abuse what is good in itself, and I believe that this rule only has the popular vice in view. These are bridles for calves, with which neither the saints — whom we hear speaking so freely about themselves — nor the philosophers, nor the theologians let themselves be curbed; and neither will I, who am as little of the one as the other. If they do not write of themselves expressly, at least when the occasion calls for it they do not hesitate to step out into the open. What does Socrates discourse on more than himself? To what does he more often direct and steer the conversation of his disciples, than to speak of themselves — not of the lesson in their book, but of the substance and motion of their souls? We confess ourselves religiously to God and our confessor; and to our neighbours, in front of everyone. But some will answer that there we say nothing but accusations against ourselves. Why then, we are saying everything; for our very virtue itself is faulty and porous. My trade and my art is to live; anyone who forbids me to speak according to my own sense, experience, and practice might as well order an architect to speak of building not from his own knowledge but from his neighbour's, by someone else's knowledge and not his own. If it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues, why does Cicero not prefer the eloquence of Hortensius, and Hortensius that of Cicero? Perhaps they mean that I should give testimony of myself by works and effects, not just by words. What I mostly paint is my thoughts, a subject without shape and incapable of producing visible results; it is all I can do to give it body in this airy form of the voice. The wisest and most devout men have lived in great care to avoid any showy effects. Effects would speak more of fortune than of me; they show their own face, not mine, and only uncertainly, by inference; they are samples of one particular virtue. I expose myself entire. It is a body in which, at a single view, the veins, muscles, and tendons all appear, each in its place — here the effects of a cold, there of a beating heart, very tentatively. I do not write my deeds; I write myself and my essence.

I think a man should be very careful how he rates himself, and equally conscientious in giving a true report — for better or worse — impartially. If I thought myself perfectly good and wise, I would shout it out for all to hear. To speak less of oneself than the truth warrants is folly, not modesty; to take a smaller coin than one's worth is, according to Aristotle, fainthearted and cowardly. No virtue helps itself out with falsehood; truth is never a matter for error. To say more about oneself than is really true is not always sheer presumption either; it is often, more than that, sheer folly: to be excessively pleased with what you are, and to fall into an indiscreet self-love, is in my opinion the heart of this vice. The most sovereign cure for it is to do the exact opposite of what those people recommend who, by forbidding men to speak of themselves, by the same act forbid them to think of themselves. Pride lives in the thought; the tongue can have only a very small part in it.

They imagine that to think of oneself is to be delighted with oneself, that to keep one's own company and converse with oneself is to indulge oneself too much; but this excess springs only in people who take a superficial view of themselves and devote their main attention to their affairs, who call it mere daydreaming and idleness to occupy oneself with oneself, and treat self-cultivation as a building of castles in the air, looking on themselves as on a third party, a stranger. If anyone is rapt by his own knowledge, looking only at those beneath him, let him just turn his eyes back to past ages, and his pride will be brought down when he finds so many thousand spirits there who trample him underfoot. If he is in flattering admiration of his personal valour, let him recall the lives of Scipio and Epaminondas — so many armies, so many nations that leave him far behind. No particular quality can rightly make a man proud, once he weighs in the same scale the many other weak and imperfect qualities he has, plus the nothingness of the human condition at large. Because Socrates alone had truly absorbed the precept of his god, "Know thyself," and by that study arrived at the perfection of taking himself for nothing, he alone was thought worthy of the title of sage. Whoever shall know himself in that way, let him say so boldly.

title: Of recompenses of honour
paragraphs: Those who write the life of Augustus Caesar note this point about his military discipline: he was wonderfully generous in giving material gifts to men of merit, but extremely sparing of the true recompenses of honour — even though his own uncle had granted him all the military honours before he had ever been in the field. It was a clever invention, adopted in most of the world's governments, to set up certain empty, intrinsically valueless distinctions to honour and reward virtue: crowns of laurel, oak, and myrtle; a particular cut of garment; the privilege of riding in a coach inside the city, or at night by torchlight; a special seat in public assemblies; the prerogative of certain additional names and titles; certain marks on a coat of arms; and the like. Their use, according to the temper of different nations, has varied, and they are still in use today.

We in France, like several of our neighbours, have orders of knighthood instituted specifically for this purpose. It is, in truth, a very good and useful custom to find some acknowledgement for the worth of rare and excellent men, and to satisfy them with rewards that cost neither prince nor people anything. And the fact, established by long experience and which we ourselves once observed, that men of quality have always been more jealous of such honours than of rewards involving gain and profit, has very good ground and reason behind it. If you mix in with the reward — which ought to be purely an honour — other goods and money on top, the mixture, instead of raising its esteem, debases and cheapens it. The Order of Saint Michael, which was long held in such repute among us, had no greater asset than this: it carried no other benefit attached to it. The result was that, formerly, there was no office or title which the gentry sought with such eagerness and affection as that one; no rank carried more respect and grandeur. Valour and worth were more eagerly drawn to, more ambitiously aimed at, a recompense purely their own — glorious rather than profitable. For other gifts have less dignity in use, because they are handed out on all sorts of occasions: with money you pay the wages of a servant, the speed of a courier, dancing, vaulting, talking, and the meanest services we receive; you even reward vices with it — flattery, treachery, pimping. No wonder, then, that virtue is less eager for, less ready to accept, this common kind of payment than one that is proper and peculiar to her, noble and generous through and through. Augustus had good reason to be more sparing with this than with material gifts, since honour is a privilege whose principal essence comes from its rarity; and virtue itself works the same way:
"Cui malus est nemo, quis bonus esse potest?"
["Where no one is bad, who can be good?" — Martial, xii. 82.]

We do not mean it as a compliment when we say that someone is careful in the education of his children, because it is a common act, however right and well done; any more than we praise a great tree where the whole forest is the same. I doubt any citizen of Sparta took much pride in his courage, since it was the universal virtue of the whole nation; or in his honesty and his contempt for riches. No recompense fits a virtue, however great, once it has become routine; and I am not sure that we can even call a thing great when it is common.

Since, then, these rewards of honour have no value or esteem beyond the fact that few people enjoy them, you only have to be generous with them to bring them down to nothing. And although there may now be more men deserving of our order than there used to be, its estimation still ought not to be lowered, nor its honour cheapened; in fact, it may easily turn out that more do deserve it, since there is no virtue that spreads as quickly as military valour. There is another virtue — the true, perfect, philosophical kind, of which I am not speaking, and the name of which I am only using in its common sense — much greater and fuller than this one: a steadiness and firmness of soul that despises all kinds of adverse accidents equally, even, uniform, and constant, of which the virtue we are discussing is only one little ray. Habit, education, example, and custom can do everything towards establishing the kind I am talking about, and can easily make it common, as the experience of our civil wars makes plain enough. Whoever could at this moment unite us all, Catholic and Huguenot, into one body and set us on some bold common enterprise would soon make our old military reputation flourish again. It is quite certain that in former times the reward of this order had its eye not only on valour but on something further: it never went to a brave soldier as such, but to a great captain; the science of obeying was not thought to deserve so honourable a prize. There was a more comprehensive military skill required for it, taking in most and the greatest qualities of a soldier:
"Neque enim eaedem militares et imperatoriae artes sunt,"
["For the arts of the soldier and of the general are not the same." — Livy, xxv. 19.]

— as well as a station in life suitable to such a dignity. But, I say, even if more men were worthy of it than formerly, it still ought not to be more freely handed out. Better to err in not giving it to people who would have deserved it than to lose for good, as we have recently done, the fruit of so useful an invention. No man of spirit will deign to take pride in something he holds in common with many; and those of our own day who have least deserved this recompense are the loudest in pretending to disdain it, so as to rank themselves with those whose particular right has been wronged by the unworthy giving away of the distinction.

Now, to think that by wiping out and abolishing this order we can suddenly create and bring into credit another like it, is not a proper undertaking for so undisciplined and sick a time as ours. The new one will from the start run into the same problems that have ruined the old. The rules for handing out this new order would need to be tightly drawn and hedged in by strict limits, in order to give it authority — and this turbulent age cannot bear such a curb. Besides, before any new one can come into repute, the memory of the first, and of the contempt into which it has fallen, must first be buried in oblivion.

This is a natural enough place to bring in some discussion of valour, and how this virtue differs from others; but since Plutarch has handled the subject so often, I would only be giving myself extra work by repeating what he has said. It is, however, worth noting that our nation puts valour, vaillance, at the top of all the virtues, as the word itself shows, deriving from valeur. In our usage, when we say a man of high worth or a good man in our court style, it means a valiant man, after the Roman fashion; for the general term for virtue with them comes from vis, force. The proper, sole, and essential profession of the French nobility is arms; and it is likely that the first virtue which showed itself among men and gave some an advantage over others was the one by which the strongest and bravest mastered the weaker and gained particular authority and reputation — hence its honoured name; or else these nations, being very warlike, gave first place to the virtue they were most familiar with. In just the same way, our own anxious obsession with the chastity of women makes the phrase a good woman, a woman of worth, a woman of honour and virtue mean nothing more than a chaste woman, as if, to bind them to that one duty, we were content to ignore all the rest and gave them free rein in all other faults, provided they avoided that one of incontinence.

title: Of the affection of fathers to their children
paragraphs: To Madame d'Estissac.

Madam, if the strangeness and novelty of my subject — which usually give things their value — do not save me, I shall never come out of this foolish attempt with any honour: but the subject is so fantastic, and so unlike anything in common usage, that this, perhaps, may carry it off. It was a melancholy mood, and consequently a mood very contrary to my natural complexion, brought on by the brooding solitude into which I have for some years now retired, that first put into my head this idle fancy of writing. Finding myself totally unprovided with any other matter, I offered myself to myself as subject and argument. It is the only book in the world of its kind, and a wild and extravagant project. Nothing about the business is worth notice except that extravagance; for in a subject so empty and frivolous, even the best workman in the world could not have given it a shape fit to recommend it for any kind of esteem.

Now, madam, having to draw my own portrait to the life, I would have left out an important feature if I had not also represented the honour I have always had for you and your merits — which I have deliberately chosen to put at the start of this chapter, because, among the many other fine qualities you possess, the tender love you have shown your children stands very high. Whoever knows at what age Monsieur d'Estissac, your husband, left you a widow; the great and honourable matches that have since been offered to you, as many as to any lady of your rank in France; the constancy and steadiness with which, for so many years, you have borne so many sharp difficulties, the burden and conduct of business that has hounded you in every corner of the kingdom, and is not yet tired of harassing you; and the happy result you have given to all of it, by your own prudence or good fortune — anyone who knows all that will easily agree with me that we have no more vivid example of maternal devotion in our times than yours. I thank God, madam, that it has been so well placed; for the great hopes that Monsieur d'Estissac your son gives of himself are firm enough that when he comes of age you will harvest from him all the obedience and gratitude of a very good man. But since, on account of his tender years, he has not been able to take in those services of the highest value which he has received from you in such number, I want, if these papers should one day come into his hands when I no longer have mouth or speech to tell him myself, that he should receive from me a true account of what is being more effectively shown to him by its effects already: namely, that there is no gentleman in France more indebted to a mother's care, and that he cannot, in the future, give better or more certain proof of his own worth and virtue than by acknowledging you for the excellent mother that you are.

If there is any law that is truly natural — that is to say, any instinct that can be seen universally and permanently imprinted in both animals and men (which is open to dispute) — I would say that, in my opinion, next to each creature's care for its own preservation and avoidance of what may hurt it, the affection which the begetter bears towards his offspring holds second place. And since nature seems to have entrusted it to us, in view of the extension and continuation of the successive pieces of her machinery, it is no wonder if, on the other side, that of children towards their parents is not as great. Add to this the Aristotelian observation that whoever does a benefit to someone loves him more than he is loved back by him; that the giver loves more than the receiver; and that every craftsman is fonder of his work than the work, if it had feeling, would be of him — since it is dear to us to be, and to be consists in motion and activity, so that every man has in some sort a being in his work. A benefactor performs a fine and honourable action; the one who receives the benefit performs only a useful action. Now the useful is far less loveable than the honourable; the honourable is stable and lasting, giving the man who has done it a continuing satisfaction. The useful slips away easily and the memory of it is neither so fresh nor so pleasant. The things dearest to us are those that have cost us most, and giving is more costly than receiving.

Since it has pleased God to give us some capacity for reason, in order that we should not, like the animals, be slavishly subject to the laws common to both, but should accept them by judgement and willing freedom, we ought, indeed, to give something to the simple authority of nature, but not let ourselves be tyrannically swept along by her; reason alone should guide our inclinations. For my part, I have an odd distaste for those impulses that are set off in us without the mediation and direction of judgement. On the subject I am dealing with, I cannot share that passion for dandling and caressing infants barely born, with neither motion of soul nor shape of body distinguishable enough to make them lovable, and I have not willingly let them be nursed near me. A true and well-regulated affection ought to be born and to grow along with our knowledge of what they are; then, if they prove worthy of it, natural inclination walking hand in hand with reason, we should cherish them with a truly fatherly love — and likewise, if they are not, we should still defer to reason in spite of the pull of nature. Most of the time it works the other way round. Usually we are more taken with the running about, the games, and the childish silliness of our children than we are, later, with their most accomplished doings — as if we had loved them as our playthings, like monkeys, and not as men; and there are some who will spend liberally to buy them toys to play with, but become very tight-fisted about the slightest necessary expense once they grow up. In fact, it looks as if jealousy at seeing them appear in and enjoy the world just as we are about to leave it makes us stingier and meaner towards them; it vexes us that they are treading on our heels, as if pushing us out. If that were really something to be feared — since the order of things is such that, to tell the truth, they cannot exist or live except at the expense of our being and life — then we ought never to have become fathers at all.

For my part, I think it cruelty and injustice not to admit them to a share of our goods and to fellowship in our domestic affairs once they are capable of it, and not to cut down our own spending to make more room for theirs, since this is what we begot them for. It is unjust that an old fellow, broken and half-dead, should alone in his chimney corner enjoy the money that would be enough to maintain and advance several children, leaving them, meanwhile, to lose their best years for want of means to make their way in public service and in the knowledge of the world. A man, by doing this, drives them to despair, and to seek out, by whatever means however dishonest, a way of supporting themselves. I have seen in my time several young men of good family so given to stealing that no correction could cure them. I knew one of a very good family to whom, at the request of a brother of his — a very honest and brave gentleman — I once spoke about this, and he answered, candidly admitting to me, that he had been driven into this shabby practice by the severity and greed of his father, but that he was now so used to it that he could not stop. And at that very time he had been caught stealing a lady's rings, having gone into her room when she was dressing along with several others. He reminded me of a story I had heard about another gentleman, so thoroughly trained in this fine trade in his youth that, after coming into his estate and resolving to give it up, he still could not keep his hands off anything he saw he liked in a shop as he passed by, even though he had to bear the shame of sending afterwards to pay for it. And I have myself seen several so habituated to this quality that even among their own friends they could not stop themselves from filching, though they meant to return what they had taken. I am a Gascon, and yet there is no vice I understand less than this one; I hate it more from temperament than I condemn it by reason. I do not even covet anything that belongs to someone else. This province of ours, in plain truth, has a rather worse reputation in this respect than the other parts of the kingdom; and yet several times in our own day we have seen men of good families from other provinces brought before the courts and convicted of abominable thefts. I am afraid this vice is, in some way, to be blamed on the same vice of the fathers I have been talking about.

And if anyone should tell me, as a very intelligent lord once did, that "he was hoarding wealth not to get any other use out of his thrift but to make himself respected and sought after by his relatives; and that, since age had robbed him of all other power, this was his only remaining means of keeping authority in the family and not being neglected and despised by all around him" — in truth, not only old age, but, according to Aristotle, every kind of weakness encourages greed; that is something, but it is medicine for a disease that a man ought to prevent the birth of. A father is very miserable who has no other hold on his children's affection than their need for his help — if that can be called affection. He must make himself worthy of respect by his virtue and wisdom, and worthy of love by his kindness and the sweetness of his manners. Even the ashes of a rich subject have their value; we treat the bones and relics of worthy men with respect and reverence. No old age can be so decrepit, in a man who has lived honourably, that it is not still venerable, especially to his children, whose souls he should have trained to their duty by reason, not by need and dependence on him, nor by harshness and compulsion:
"Et errat longe mea quidem sententia Qui imperium credat esse gravius, aut stabilius, Vi quod fit, quam illud, quod amicitia adjungitur."
["He is much mistaken, in my opinion, who thinks that government more weighty and lasting which rests on force, than that which is held together by friendship." — Terence, Adelphoe, i. 1, 40.]

I condemn all violence in the upbringing of a tender soul designed for honour and freedom. There is something servile about rigour and constraint, and I hold that what cannot be done by reason, prudence, and tact will never be done by force. I myself was raised that way; they tell me that in all my early years I felt the rod only twice, and then very lightly. I have used the same method with my own children, all of whom died at nurse except Léonore, my only daughter, who reached the age of five and more with no other correction for her childish faults (her mother's indulgence readily seconding mine) than words, and very gentle ones at that. Even if my hopes were entirely disappointed in this method, there would be plenty of other causes to lay the fault on without blaming my discipline, which I know to be natural and just; and I would have been still more scrupulous on this point with sons, as less born to subjection and more free, and I would have made it my business to fill their hearts with openness and freedom. I have never observed any other effects of whipping than to make boys either more cowardly or more wilfully stubborn.
Do we wish to be loved by our children? Do we want to remove from them every occasion for wishing our death — though no occasion for so horrible a wish could ever be just or excusable?
"Nullum scelus rationem habet."
["No wickedness has any reason behind it." — Livy, xxviii. 28]

Let us reasonably accommodate their lives with what is in our power. To do this, we should not marry so young that our age is practically confused with theirs; for this disadvantage plunges us into many very great difficulties, especially among the gentry, who are in a station with little to do and live on their rents alone. Elsewhere, among people who live by their work, the multitude and company of children is an addition to the common stock; they are so many new tools and instruments to grow rich with.

I married at thirty-three, and I agree with the opinion fixing the right age at thirty-five, which is said to be Aristotle's. Plato would have nobody marry before thirty, but he has reason to laugh at those who took up marriage after fifty-five, and condemns their offspring as unworthy of food and life. Thales gave the truest limits: when, as a young man, his mother kept urging him to marry, he answered, "It is too soon," and, when he was getting on in years and pressed again, "It is too late." A man must deny opportunity to every inopportune action. The ancient Gauls held it a horrible thing for a man to keep company with a woman before he was twenty, and strongly recommended to men intending themselves for war that they keep their virginity well into their grown years, since courage is sapped and diverted by intercourse with women:
"Ma, or congiunto a giovinetta sposa, E lieto omai de' figli, era invilito Negli affetti di padre et di marito."
["But now, married to a young wife and happy in his children, he had been weakened by the feelings of father and husband." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, x. 39.]

Muley Hassan, king of Tunis, the one whom the Emperor Charles V restored to his kingdom, reproached the memory of his father Mahomet with his frequenting of women, calling him loose, effeminate, and a begetter of children. The Greek histories tell us that Iccus the Tarentine, Chryso, Astyllus, Diopompos, and others, to keep their bodies in shape for the Olympic games and similar exercises, denied themselves during that training all dealings with Venus. In a certain country of the Spanish Indies men were not allowed to marry until after forty, yet the girls were given over at ten. It is not time for a gentleman of thirty to give place to his son of twenty; he is himself in a position to serve both in war and in the court of his prince; he needs all his resources; and yet, no doubt, he ought to surrender a share — but not so great a share as to forget himself for others. For such a man, the answer fathers usually have at the ready — "I will not take off my clothes before I go to bed" — serves well enough.

But a father worn out by age and infirmities, and cut off by weakness and ill health from the common society of men, wrongs both himself and his family by piling up a great heap of treasure. He has lived long enough, if he is wise, to be willing to undress for bed — not down to the shirt, I admit, but down to it and a good warm dressing-gown; the rest of the pomps, of which he has no further use, he should voluntarily hand over to those to whom, in the order of nature, they belong. It is only reasonable that he should let them have the use of those things, since nature has put him in a state in which he can no longer enjoy them himself; otherwise there is plainly malice and envy in the business. The greatest action of the Emperor Charles V was this: in imitation of some of the ancients of his own rank, recognising that it is reasonable to strip ourselves when our clothes are loading us down and grown too heavy, and to lie down when our legs begin to give way, he resigned his possessions, his greatness, and his power to his son, when he found his vigour and steadiness for the conduct of affairs were failing in a way unworthy of the glory he had won in them:
"Solve senescentem mature sanus equum, ne Peccet ad extremum ridendus, et ilia ducat."
["Dismiss the ageing horse in good time, while you are still sound, lest he stumble in the lists at the end, panting, and the spectators laugh." — Horace, Epistles, i. 1, 8.]

This fault — of not noticing in good time and not feeling the weakness and great alteration that age naturally brings on both body and mind (which, in my opinion, are equal, if indeed the soul does not get more than half) — has cost most of the great men in the world their reputation. I have known in my time, and been on familiar terms with, people of great authority whom one could plainly see had slipped marvellously below the level of competence I knew they once had, judging by the reputation they had built up in their earlier years; I could heartily, for their own sakes, have wished them at home and at ease, freed of public or military positions that had grown too heavy for their shoulders. I was once on very familiar terms in a gentleman's house, the master a widower and very old, though healthy and cheerful enough. He had several daughters to marry off and a son already grown, which brought him a great many visitors and a great deal of expense, neither of which pleased him — not only out of frugality but still more because, on account of his age, he had moved into a way of life very different from ours. I told him one day a little boldly, as I was used to doing, that he would do better to give us younger folk room, and to leave his principal house (for it was his only well-placed and well-furnished one) to his son, while he himself retired to an estate he had nearby, where nobody would disturb his peace; since otherwise he could not avoid being pestered by us, given the situation of his children.
